B.	Proposed post and non-post resource requirements for 2027
Overview

The United Nations Joint Staff Pension Fund was established by the General Assembly in 1949 to provide retirement, death, disability and related benefits to the staff of the United Nations and such other organizations as might be admitted to its membership. In accordance with the regulations adopted by the Assembly, the Pension Fund is administered by the United Nations Joint Staff Pension Board, a staff pension committee for each member organization and a secretariat of the Pension Board and each such committee.

The expenses incurred by the staff pension committee in the administration of the regulations of a member organization are met by the general budget of that organization. However, given that the central secretariat of the Pension Fund grew out of the secretariat of the United Nations Staff Pension Committee, it continued to handle pension administration for the United Nations by special arrangement with the Pension Board. For those services, the United Nations reimburses the Pension Fund in accordance with the cost-sharing arrangement, as approved by the General Assembly in its resolution 75/246.

At the time that the present report was being prepared, the proposed budget of the Pension Fund for 2027 had not been finalized. The estimates will be subject to further revision in accordance with the administrative budget of the Pension Fund for 2027 and action taken by the General Assembly at its eighty-first session on the basis of the recommendations that the Pension Board may make in 2026 with respect to that budget. A statement of administrative and budgetary implications will be submitted to the Assembly at its eighty-first session should the Pension Board’s recommendations involve resources different from those estimated in the present report.

text: II.	Secretary-General

children.text: B.	Proposed post and non-post resource requirements for 2027
Overview

In accordance with Article 97 of the Charter of the United Nations, the Secretary-General, who is appointed by the General Assembly on the recommendation of the Security Council and who, in turn, appoints the staff, is the Chief Administrative Officer of the Organization. The Secretary-General also has an important political function by virtue of Article 99 of the Charter and a role in all United Nations meetings and such other functions as are entrusted to him by other principal organs of the Organization, as provided for in Article 98.

As the Chief Administrative Officer of the Organization, the Secretary-General is entrusted with a broad range of responsibilities under the Charter. Within the sphere of competence of the office, the Secretary-General takes action, on his or her own initiative, on a wide range of political, economic, social and humanitarian questions, reporting to and requesting guidance from the General Assembly and the Security Council, as appropriate. The Secretary-General uses his or her best efforts to assist in settling disputes between States and may bring to the attention of the Council any matter that may threaten the maintenance of international peace and security. Moreover, the Secretary-General plays a key role in efforts to ensure the observance of human rights. The Secretary-General provides policy direction to the departments, offices and other organizational units of the Secretariat in the execution of their functions and guidance and coordination to the programmes and other elements of the Organization. In addition, as Chair of the United Nations System Chief Executives Board for Coordination (CEB), the Secretary-General has a coordinating function in relation to the entire United Nations system of organizations. The activities of the Secretary-General in 2027 will be directed towards the achievement of the priorities of the Organization.

text: III.	Executive direction and management

children.text: The proposed resources under executive direction and management would provide for the Executive Office of the Secretary-General and the offices of the Directors-General of the United Nations Offices at Geneva, Vienna and Nairobi. Those offices provide support to the Secretary-General in his capacity as Chief Administrative Officer of the United Nations under Article 97 of the Charter of the United Nations by assisting in: (a) the establishment of general policy and in the exercise of executive direction in relation to the work of the Secretariat, the United Nations funds and programmes and other entities within the Organization; (b) the supervision and coordination of the work of the Organization pursuant to the decisions of the Secretary-General and to the relevant directives of the intergovernmental bodies concerned; (c) relations with the press and the public; (d) inter-agency coordination functions in relation to the United Nations system of organizations, regional organizations and non-governmental organizations (NGOs); (e) relations with the principal organs of the United Nations and host Governments; and (f) contacts with Governments and delegations pursuant to Articles 98 and 99 of the Charter. Further details are provided under the relevant components. The proposed level of resources provides for the full, efficient and effective implementation of mandates.
1.	Executive Office of the Secretary-General
B.	Proposed post and non-post resource requirements for 2027
Overview

The Executive Office of the Secretary-General provides assistance to the Secretary-General in the establishment of general policy, in the executive direction, coordination and expeditious performance of the work of the Secretariat and of the programmes and other elements of the Organization, and in contacts with Governments, delegations, the press and the public. It provides further assistance to the Secretary-General in strategic planning, the preparation of the annual report of the Organization and the annual report on the rule of law, political, economic and inter-agency affairs, liaison and representation functions and the fulfilment of the priorities and mandates set out by the General Assembly. The resources of the Office also provide for the post of Deputy Secretary-General, whose functions and responsibilities are defined in paragraph 1 of Assembly resolution 52/12 B.

The Executive Office functions as an integrated office, with reporting lines through the Deputy Secretary-General and Chef de Cabinet to the Secretary-General. The units within the Executive Office work as a team to support the Secretary-General and the activities of the principals regardless of their direct reporting lines. The resources for the Office provide for post and non-post resources in support of the activities of the Secretary-General. The overall number of posts approved for 2027 remains unchanged.

In accordance with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, in particular target 12.6 of the Sustainable Development Goals, in which organizations are encouraged to integrate sustainability information into their reporting cycles, and in compliance with the cross-cutting mandate set out in paragraph 19 of General Assembly resolution 72/219, the Executive Office has continued to integrate environmental management practices into its operations to ensure resource efficiencies, waste reduction and system-wide behavioural changes across the UN. In 2025, the Office continued to implement management changes to lower its carbon and resource footprint, by further streamlining correspondences and document processing workflows, and incentivizing less print material as a good office practice. The recycling of event content and media branding was also promoted. Following General Assembly resolution 77/161 on Promoting zero-waste initiatives to advance the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, the Executive Office has helped to raise awareness of waste reduction measures across daily processes, while advocating for more circularity and resource efficiency in office initiatives and procurement of services.

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy launched by the Secretary-General in 2019, the Executive Office continues to champion system-wide efforts to advance the inclusion of persons with disabilities. The Executive Office strives to make the reports of the Secretary-General issued by the Office accessible to persons with disabilities. For example, the report of the Secretary-General on the Work of the Organization was published in accessible formats, including ePub and Easy Read. In 2025, the Executive Office enhanced accessibility of the United Nations General Assembly High-Level Week, with provision of International Sign interpretation and live captioning at the SDG Moment.  In 2027, the Executive Office will continue its efforts to ensure, where feasible, that reports, communications and events of the Secretary-General are accessible. The Executive Office is also taking active steps to ensure the provision of reasonable accommodation to staff members with disabilities and will continue such efforts in 2027.
Deputy Secretary-General

The Deputy Secretary-General, whose functions and responsibilities are defined in paragraph 1 of Assembly resolution 52/12 B, will continue to play a central leadership role in ensuring coherence and strategic direction across the UN development system. The Deputy Secretary-General supports the Secretary‑General in elevating the Organization’s impact in the economic, social, and environmental spheres, while also reinforcing linkages with humanitarian activities, peace and security and human rights pillars. Through sustained engagement with Member States, regional organizations, international financial institutions, and diverse stakeholders she helps garner attention and resources towards sustainable development.  As Chair of the United Nations Sustainable Development Group, the Deputy Secretary-General convenes the executive heads of all UN development entities and directly oversees the Development Coordination Office. The Deputy Secretary-General guides coordinated efforts to advance the Sustainable Development agenda, including implementation of intergovernmentally agreed frameworks, such as the Sevilla Commitment of the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, the Paris Agreement on climate change, relevant components of the Pact for the Future, and the Doha Political Declaration of the Second World Summit for Social Development. The Deputy Secretary-General also leads the implementation of all mandates to reposition the United Nations development system. Within EOSG, she directly supervises the Sustainable Development Unit, while also chairing the Rule of Law Coordination and Resource Group.
Chef de Cabinet

The Chef de Cabinet supports the Secretary-General in the execution of his political role and engagements. The Chef de Cabinet acts as an interface with Member States and, on behalf of the Secretary-General, primarily with the General Assembly and the Security Council. In addition, the Chef de Cabinet oversees the administrative and management portfolio, senior leadership appointments and the implementation of the management reforms, peace and security reforms, and other reforms as requested by the Secretary-General, as well as the alignment of the various reform streams. The Chef de Cabinet also oversees the efforts of the Organization to advance equitable geographical distribution and gender parity, to prevent sexual exploitation and abuse and to address racism within the Organization. The Chef de Cabinet chairs the Management Committee, the Management Performance Board, the High-level Steering Group on preventing sexual exploitation and abuse and the Senior Emergency Policy Team. The Chef de Cabinet also oversees the work of, and substantive support provided to those bodies and the Standing Principals’ Group. The Chef de Cabinet provides direction and oversees the overall management of the Executive Office of the Secretary-General and directly oversees the Political, Peacekeeping, Humanitarian and Human Rights Unit, the Strategic Communication and Speech Writing Unit, the Office of the Spokesperson, the Senior Leadership Appointment Team and the Central Record Unit.
Office of the Secretary-General

The Office of the Secretary-General provides support and assistance to the Secretary-General. The Office liaises with the Deputy Secretary General, and the Chef de Cabinet, and conveys the Secretary General’s guidance. It reviews and clears documentation, correspondence, notes, letters, reports and statements. The Office oversees the scheduling of meetings and events, the preparation of scenarios and the travel of the Secretary-General, and is responsible for preparation for scheduled activities, including consolidating background notes, key messages, remarks and speeches, and liaising with permanent missions.
Central Records Unit

The Central Records Unit manages all incoming correspondence for the Secretary-General and EOSG Principals, including the Deputy Secretary-General, Chef de Cabinet, and Unit Chiefs. It also provides records management services and advice to EOSG staff on information sensitivity handling, document management and quick reference.
Senior Leadership Appointment Team

The Senior Leadership Appointments Team applies expert institutional knowledge to produce well-informed advice to the Chef de Cabinet in managing the appointments of senior leadership for the approval of the Secretary-General. Senior leadership appointments refer to those appointments at the Under-Secretary-General, Assistant Secretary-General and Director level.
Office of the Spokesperson

The Office of the Spokesperson for the Secretary-General provides information to the media on the work of the Secretary-General and the United Nations system as a whole through daily briefings, direct responses to media enquiries, press conferences, background briefings and interviews with the Secretary-General, the Deputy Secretary-General and other senior officials. The Office provides advice on media relations to the Secretary-General, the Deputy Secretary-General and United Nations officials. Personnel of the Office travel with the Secretary-General, keep him abreast of breaking news, interact with media to ensure coverage of the activities of the Secretary-General, and ensure that all statements made are placed on record.
Political, Peacekeeping, Humanitarian and Human Rights Unit

The responsibilities of the Political, Peacekeeping, Humanitarian and Human Rights Unit include working closely with the relevant line departments to provide situational awareness, trend analysis and advice on emerging and ongoing issues of interest and concern across the political, peacekeeping, humanitarian and human rights portfolios; supporting senior management decision-making on country situations and relevant thematic files; ensuring effective and coordinated United Nations system analysis, reporting and response on situations of interest and concern; ensuring policy oversight and quality assurance of various communications and reports of the Secretary-General on political, peacekeeping, humanitarian or human rights issues; providing high-quality and well-coordinated input to public and private communications; and ensuring that human rights concerns are adequately reflected in the above-mentioned work. The Unit also plays a critical role in supporting the Secretary-General in the implementation of the relevant Peace and Security Actions in the Pact for the Future.
Rule of Law Unit

The Rule of Law Unit acts as a catalyst of action in strengthening United Nations activities to promote the rule of law. The Unit serves as the focal point in the Executive Office for legal questions, the rule of law, counter-terrorism and the prevention of violent extremism, international justice and accountability, organized crime and drugs, transitional justice, anti-corruption, and provides support for the system-wide coordination, coherence and quality of rule of law activities of the United Nations. It develops system-wide strategies, policy direction, best practice materials and guidance for the Organization in promoting the fundamental importance of the rule of law. The Unit provides quality assurance of, and input for, various communications and reports of the Secretary-General on rule of law issues. Moreover, the Unit provides support to the Rule of Law Coordination and Resource Group in carrying out the tasks set out in the related report of the Secretary-General (A/61/636-S/2006/980) and implementing the New Vision of the Secretary-General for the Rule of Law, and leads the preparation of the Secretary-General’s annual report on the rule of law.
Scheduling and Travel Unit

The Scheduling and Travel Unit oversees the scheduling of meetings, events and travel of the Secretary-General, handling requests for invitations and individual meetings in consultation with departments, offices and units. The responsibilities of the Unit include preparation for scheduled activities (meetings, events and travel), including the consolidation of briefing materials, the preparation of scenarios and the organization of the travel of the Secretary-General.
Strategic Communication and Speech Writing Unit

The Strategic Communication and Speech Writing Unit provides communications advice and support to the Secretary-General. The unit drafts speeches, video messages, op-ed articles and other materials for delivery by the Secretary-General. The unit also works with communications colleagues and others across the United Nations system on strategic planning and crisis communications; helps formulate key messaging; ensures that the Secretary-General’s speeches and messages are disseminated as widely as possible; and provides speech support to the Deputy Secretary-General and other senior officials in the Executive Office.
Strategic Planning and Monitoring Unit

The Strategic Planning and Monitoring Unit provides support for strategic decision-making, priority-setting, forward planning, analysis and advice, and risk as well as change management to foster alignment across the United Nations system, including on science and emerging and frontier issues. The Unit ensures strategic direction and coherence in planning frameworks; supports analyses, reviews, assessments and plans for integrated United Nations response efforts, with a focus on crisis-affected and fragile settings, including the preparation of strategic options for engagement based on information from the United Nations system. The Unit translates the guidance of the Secretary-General into strategic directives. The unit supports institutional coherence on system-wide capabilities in artificial intelligence, data, digital, foresight and behavioral science areas to support the organization, in offering solutions to the challenges of the twenty-first century.
Pact for the Future Implementation Team

The Team for Pact Implementation was established following the Summit of the Future to coordinate, facilitate and support the UN System’s implementation of the Pact for the Future and its annexes — the Global Digital Compact and the Declaration on Future Generations. This includes serving as the secretariat to the Pact Steering Committee, chaired by the Secretary-General; tracking and reporting on implementation efforts across the UN system; and ensuring clear communication of progress. The Team also supports regular engagement with Member States, and a broad range of stakeholders — in partnership with relevant UN entities — to advance implementation efforts. Finally, the Team works closely with relevant Secretariat entities to lay the groundwork to support Member States’ formal reviews of the Pact and its annexes in 2027 and 2028, helping to ensure these milestones are substantive, inclusive and forward-looking.
Sustainable Development Unit

The Sustainable Development Unit supports strategic engagement on sustainable development, guided by the 2030 Agenda, the Addis Ababa Action Agenda and Seville Commitment, the Paris Agreement and other relevant intergovernmentally agreed commitments. The Unit supports the Secretary-General and Deputy Secretary-General in mobilizing ambition and action aimed at accelerating SDG progress. The Unit has helped shape the narrative on key global issues and sharpened the UN system’s focus on catalytic SDG transitions that unlock transformative policy change and finance at scale. Priority areas under the responsibility of the Unit include financing for development; energy, climate action and environmental sustainability; digitalisation, food systems, jobs and social protection, global health, water and sanitation, education, and migration and development. The Unit’s work is anchored in cross pillar collaboration and the intrinsic link between peace, stability and sustainable development. Under the Leave No One Behind pillar, priority attention is consistently given to gender equality, youth engagement, and the inclusion of persons with disabilities, Indigenous Peoples, and local communities. The work of the Unit remains instrumental in supporting the implementation of the Pact for the Future, consolidating the United Nations development system’s repositioning, and strengthening a culture of collaboration across the system as well as with external stakeholders and partners.

text: IV.	Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Children and Armed Conflict

children.text: A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Children and Armed Conflict is responsible for the protection of children affected by armed conflict and for advocating to end and prevent the six grave violations against children identified by the Security Council from occurring in the first place. The six grave violations are the denial of humanitarian access for children (resolution 1261 (1999)); the recruitment and use of children (resolution 1379 (2001)); the killing and maiming of children (resolution 1882 (2009)); rape and other forms of sexual violence against children (ibid.); attacks on schools and hospitals (resolution 1998 (2011)); and the abduction of children (resolution 2225 (2015)). The Office of the Special Representative works primarily in the situations of armed conflict or of concern identified in the annual report of the Secretary-General on children and armed conflict. The Office covers 22 situations in 5 geographical regions and promotes enhanced monitoring and reporting at the subregional level in the Lake Chad basin and central Sahel regions, in accordance with the report of the Secretary-General on children and armed conflict in 2025 (A/79/878-S/2025/247).

The mandate was established by the General Assembly in its resolution 51/77, in which the Assembly outlined key priorities of the mandate of the Special Representative, which were further formulated and shaped in subsequent Assembly resolutions and decisions, including resolution 58/245, as well as Security Council resolution 1261 (1999) and subsequent Council resolutions. The key elements of the mandate of the Special Representative are therefore to: (a) provide political leadership and high-level advocacy for the improved protection of children affected by armed conflict; (b) lead the collection of information and reporting on the plight of these children; (c) advocate, build awareness of and give prominence to ending and preventing grave violations; (d) work with United Nations partners, Member States, civil society and pertinent intergovernmental bodies to propose ideas, undertake research and facilitate discussions on the best approaches to enhance the protection response for children in situations of armed conflict, including through improved accountability processes; (e) undertake diplomatic engagement with parties to armed conflict and affected Member States in order to secure commitments to end and prevent violations against children; and (f) facilitate the work of operational child protection actors on the ground through the development and promotion of best practices, such as ensuring that child protection issues are included in peace processes, appropriate release procedures are in place, reintegration programmes are strengthened to avoid re-recruitment opportunities, child protection expertise and capacity are reinforced, and regional and national prevention plans and policies against the six grave violations are promoted.

By its resolution 80/190, the General Assembly recommended that the Secretary-General extend the mandate of the Special Representative for an additional period of four years, until 2029. As of 2027, it is proposed that a single post will serve a dual role, concurrently comprising the responsibilities of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Children and Armed Conflict and the Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Violence against Children, with one incumbent heading the two distinct offices focused on their respective mandates.
Programme of work
Objective

The objective, to which the Office contributes, is to eradicate the six grave violations committed against children in situations of armed conflict through strengthened mechanisms for the protection of children used in armed conflict, prevent these violations from occurring in the first place, and improve measures to better protect children in situations of armed conflict, including by ensuring that children are placed at the centre of peace negotiations and securing optimal conditions for the release and reintegration of children, thereby avoiding re-recruitment and contributing to sustainable peace.
Strategy and external factors for 2027

To contribute to the objective, the Office will strengthen mechanisms for the protection of children used in armed conflict, prevent these violations from occurring in the first place, and improve measures to better protect conflict-affected children. Specifically, the Office will:

(a)	Monitor and report on violations against children in situations of armed conflict through the reinforcement of existing child protection capacities on the ground and facilitate information exchanges to identify and mitigate trends in the use of children in  armed conflict, including during transition phases of relevant United Nations peace operations, in line with Security Council resolution 2764 (2024), the most recent Council resolution on children and armed conflict;

(b)	Enhance its diplomatic engagement, including through direct dialogue and/or country visits by the Special Representative, with parties to armed conflict to promote ending and preventing the use and abuse of children, and continue to advocate the protection of children affected by conflict and the prevention of grave violations against them through analysis, public outreach and targeted support, as well as the development of groups of friends of the mandate in affected States and regions;

(c)	Develop community, national, subregional and regional prevention plans, as well as other preventive measures, guided by Security Council resolutions 2427 (2018) and 2601 (2021), while promoting the adoption of international norms and standards for the protection of children by Member States;

(d)	Analyse the best practices emerging from ongoing activities to stop grave violations committed against children and promote the continued roll-out of specific public awareness campaigns in all countries and regions where there is active armed conflict and, whenever possible, in all official languages of the United Nations;

(e)	Develop curricula with partners, conduct training for defence and security personnel and assist in capacity-building for governing structures, United Nations partners, academics and civil society;

(f)	Undertake research into the six grave violations, with a focus on recruitment and use of children, provide guidelines, as relevant, to assist in their monitoring, promote the comprehensive discussion of reintegration needs and promote the inclusion of child protection issues into peace processes;

(g)	Organize and participate in seminars, workshops, conferences and other relevant meetings, including with regard to the implementation of the Pact for the Future and the working group on peace and security, to raise awareness of child protection and prevention best practices and proposed best international standards on the protection and release of children who are victims of the six grave violations;

(h)	Enhance data analysis and information management capacity to better capture the differentiated protection needs of children, including on the basis of age, gender and disability, and whether they are on the move, internally displaced, refugees or victims of cross-border trafficking, and the factors that can exacerbate their vulnerability, such as climate change, poverty and inequality, the proliferation of and illicit trafficking in arms, the impact of landmines, explosive remnants of war and improvised explosive devices, and the impact of new technologies.

(i)	Support Member States in making progress towards the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals, including Goals 3, 4, 5 and 8, in particular target 8.7 on the eradication of child labour, including the recruitment and use of child soldiers; Goals 10 and 16, in particular target 16.2 on ending abuse, exploitation, trafficking and all forms of violence against and torture of children; and Goal 17, in particular target 17.18 on enhancing capacity-building support to increase significantly the availability of high-quality, timely and reliable data disaggregated by income, gender, age, race, ethnicity, migratory status, disability, geographical location and other characteristics.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:

(a)	A decrease in the number of violations committed against children in armed conflict and an increase in the number of children released by armed forces and groups and reintegrated, including through repatriation and removal from situations of armed conflict, in line with the commitments agreed to in action plans, handover and release protocols, other commitments and mutually agreed practices;

(b)	Stronger national and regional protection and prevention systems and accountability mechanisms through justice, remediation and reparation processes, involving Member States, to address gaps in knowledge, common standards and procedures for dealing with children under threat;
(c)	Strengthened efforts to protect children, including those threatened by intercommunal violence and the emergence of new parties to armed conflict, and specific groups of children at risk;
(d)	Increased mitigation capacity of Governments to prevent violations and ensure equal access to and the continuation of education in conflict;

(e)	An international political consensus that tailored, systematic and sustainable reintegration support should be provided to all released children, including those repatriated or removed from armed conflict zones, and that child protection issues should be included in all peace processes, in order to break the cycle of violence;

(f)	Enhanced capacity of Member States and United Nations country task forces on monitoring and reporting, and their equivalents in countries where there is no monitoring and reporting mechanism in place, to support children and vulnerable communities on the ground and to ensure the continuity, effectiveness and sustainability of child protection activities, including during mission transitions or withdrawals;

(g)	Increased participation of children in decision-making processes relating to issues that have an impact on them, including their protection and reintegration needs, in accordance with the Convention on the Rights of the Child.
With regard to external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:

(a)	The political environment would be supportive for the improved measures put in place to end and prevent violations committed against children in situations of armed conflict in all situations of the children and armed conflict agenda;

(b)	The political environment would be supportive of international human rights law, in particular the rights of the child, and international humanitarian law, in particular the special respect and protections afforded to children;
(c)	The dynamics of contemporary armed conflict in which children are normally victimized allow for access to monitor and assist in the implementation of these measures.

With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, the Office will continue to garner support for the protection of children in armed conflict, including through engagement with Member States and groups of friends on children and armed conflict, to keep the plight of conflict-affected children high on the global political agenda and to advocate the ratification and implementation of the Convention on the Rights of the Child and its Optional Protocol on the involvement of children in armed conflict, and the endorsement of political commitments. The Office will reinforce partnerships with regional and subregional actors for the adoption of measures to prevent grave violations before they occur and engage with mediation actors to encourage the inclusion of child protection issues in mediation and peace processes. The Office will also work closely with civil society organizations, communities, academia and research institutes to build expertise and raise awareness of the protection of children in armed conflict.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Office will continue to support country task forces on monitoring and reporting on grave violations against children and engage with parties to conflict to strengthen advocacy for the adoption of measures to end and prevent these violations, including through capacity-building initiatives. The Office will continue to support the dissemination  of technical guidelines through the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism Technical Reference Group, an inter‑agency group bringing together the Office, the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), the Department of Peace Operations and the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs to provide guidance to United Nations partners implementing the mandate in the field. The Office will also support the exchange of information within the Task Force on Children and Armed Conflict at United Nations Headquarters. In addition, the Office will continue to strengthen its cooperation with the Offices of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Violence against Children and the Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Sexual Violence in Conflict, notably on monitoring and reporting on sexual violence affecting children, through information exchange, common messaging and joint events and initiatives, for a more effective and coordinated advocacy to ensure that the plight of conflict-affected children is visible on the international agenda.

The Office integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate. In 2027, the Office will continue to mainstream a gender perspective into the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism to strengthen its gender-sensitive analyses of grave violations against children in armed conflict, including through enhanced data analysis and support for the capacity-building activities of its field partners. The Office will follow up on the outcomes of a specialized workshop delivered to country task forces on monitoring and reporting in 2023 through a review of the draft tipsheet for strengthening gender analysis in monitoring and reporting and examine the operationalization of the workshop’s report and recommendations within the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism Technical Reference Group, which provides guidance to field-based United Nations monitors of grave violations committed against children in armed conflict. The Special Representative will continue advocacy for the protection of girls’ education from attacks, including within the framework of the endorsement and implementation of the Safe Schools Declaration. The Office will also ensure that the platforms that it creates, alongside partners, will allow for the voices of children to be heard in relevant forums and for the differentiated experience between girls and boys to be highlighted. Wherever possible, the Office will mainstream a gender perspective and examine the intersection between gender and other factors in the research that it conducts and the lessons learned and best practices that it collects and disseminates on the protection of conflict-affected children. The Office will also develop a concise policy aimed at more systematically integrating a gender perspective into its work.

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the Office will strengthen its efforts to address the protection requirements of children with disabilities in armed conflict. The Office will build on the discussion paper on the protection of children with disabilities in armed conflict published in 2023 by continuing to disseminate its conclusions and advocating with partners for the implementation of its recommendations, including the strengthening of data collection on children with disabilities in armed conflict; the consultation of persons with disabilities, including children, and the organizations that represent them; and the provision of awareness-raising and capacity-building initiatives on disability inclusion. The Office will continue its advocacy efforts to raise awareness of the plight of children with disabilities in armed conflict, and mainstream disability inclusion and its intersection with other diversity factors.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative
The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects efforts of the programme to implement all mandates in a more efficient and effective manner.

The Office will be guided by any future decisions taken in the context of the UN80 Initiative, in accordance with the applicable rules and procedures, including decisions, resolutions and established practice of the competent intergovernmental organs. This includes any decisions concerning the proposal for a single post to serve a dual role, concurrently comprising the responsibilities of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Children and Armed Conflict and the Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Violence against Children, as part of the review of thematic and geographic envoys.
Evaluation activities
An OIOS evaluation of children and armed conflict in peacekeeping operations, completed 2025, has guided the proposed programme plan for 2027.

In response to the results of the evaluation referenced above, the Office will initiate the review of handover of the political tasks related to the children and armed conflict mandate during mission drawdown, withdrawal and exit through the Technical Reference Group at Headquarters (consisting of the Office, as well as the Department of Peace Operations, the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs and the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) ), including the review of existing guidelines.
Programme performance in 2025
Decrease in the verified number of children in detention

As stipulated in article 37 (b) of the Convention on the Rights of the Child, the detention of children should only be used as a measure of last resort and for the shortest appropriate period of time. While it is not one of the six grave violations against children in armed conflict, the number of children deprived of liberty for alleged or actual association with parties to conflict remains a significant concern, as detention may expose children to further protection risks, impede their recovery and reintegration and undermine efforts to treat children associated with parties to conflict primarily as victims entitled to protection and reintegration support, in line with Security Council resolution 2427 (2018). The Office has engaged in sustained advocacy with Member States and with parties to conflict to adopt specific measures to end and prevent the detention of children for association with parties to conflict, such as the establishment of handover protocols to civilian child protection actors. In contexts like Haiti and Yemen, for example, the adoption and implementation of handover protocol for the transfer of children allegedly associated with armed groups led to the actual release of dozens of detained children to civilian actors. In the DRC, Nigeria, and Somalia, engagement with the authorities led to the transfer of children to civilian actors for reintegration purposes. The Office also monitors and reports on the number of children deprived of liberty for alleged or actual association with parties to conflict. After a sharp increase in 2024 due to the emergence of new conflicts and the intensification of existing conflict situations, the verified number of children in detention declined in 2025, notwithstanding deteriorating political and security conditions across several situations on the children and armed conflict agenda.

Planned results for 2027

Result 1: increase in the signature of action plans, handover protocols and other commitments between the United Nations and parties to conflict to end and prevent grave violations against children – Programme performance in 2025 and target for 2027

The Office’s work contributed to the adoption and implementation of measures to protect children in countries on the children and armed conflict agenda, including steps which could lead to the signature of action plans such as in Myanmar and the Sudan, which did not meet the planned target of 1 additional action plan signed in 2025. The target was not met because although three action plans were under discussion in three different contexts, the listed parties had not yet agreed to their adoption by the end of 2025.

Result 2: decrease in the number of children recruited and used by parties to conflict in situations of armed conflict – Programme performance in 2025 and target for 2027

The programme’s work contributed to a decrease in the number of children recruited or used by parties to conflict in situations of armed conflict to 6,565 children, which did not meet the planned target of 6,500 children. Despite the progress achieved, the target was not met due to escalating conflicts in situations on the children and armed conflict agenda.

Result 3: more children released from armed forces and armed groups – Proposed programme plan for 2027

The recruitment and use of children in armed conflict constitutes one of the six grave violations identified by the Security Council and remains a core focus of the Office’s monitoring, reporting and engagement with parties to conflict. Most action plans and related commitments concluded between the United Nations and parties to conflict include provisions for the release of children, the establishment of handover protocols to ensure their safe transfer to child protection actors, and measures to prevent future recruitment.  To support partners involved in the reintegration of children formerly associated with armed forces and groups, the Office, in partnership with UNESCO, published guidance for teachers and educators, aiming to equip them with the skills and knowledge to understand and address these children’s complex education needs and support their reintegration into society.
Lessons learned and planned change

The lesson for the Office, based on its research and the experience of its partners delivering reintegration programming, was that the timely release of children, their safe handover to child protection services, and the provision of reintegration support are essential peacebuilding measures. These interventions help prevent relapse into conflict, contribute to post-conflict recovery, long-term peace and sustainable development. In applying the lesson, the Office will intensify direct engagement with parties to conflict and reinforce support to United Nations partners, through capacity-building and efforts to maintain or strengthen child protection presence on the ground, in order to secure the release and handover of children. It will also advance the operationalization of its guidance for teachers and educators, including by disseminating the guidance among policymakers and United Nations partners, while engaging with conflict-affected countries to support its rollout and practical application. The Office will also enhance advocacy to promote the integration of comprehensive measures for prevention, protection, justice, and reparation for child victims in a future convention on the prevention and punishment of crimes against humanity.

children.text: A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Sexual Violence in Conflict is responsible, in line with Security Council resolution 1888 (2009), for providing coherent and strategic leadership and promoting the coordination of efforts among relevant stakeholders, through primarily the United Nations Action against Sexual Violence in Conflict, on preventing and addressing sexual violence as a weapon of war and tactic of terrorism and for engaging with justice and security sectors, all parties to armed conflict, civil society and the survivors of such crimes.

The mandate derives from the priorities established in relevant General Assembly resolutions and/or decisions, including resolution 65/259, by which the Assembly established the Office, following the establishment of the mandate of the Special Representative pursuant to Security Council resolution 1888 (2009). In accordance with resolution 1888 (2009) and subsequent related resolutions and recognizing that conflict-related sexual violence remains underreported and insufficiently addressed, the role of the Special Representative and that of the Office is, among others: (a) to give victims and affected communities a voice; (b) to mobilize the political will and action of the international community, in particular to address the impunity of perpetrators of violations; (c) to foster collaboration and partnerships and broaden the circle of stakeholders on the issue; (d) to coordinate advocacy and programmatic responses, in particular in the United Nations system; (e) to ensure more reliable and comprehensive data on sexual violence in conflict as a basis for action at all levels; and (f) to disseminate information/knowledge on approaches and best practices to address sexual violence in conflict.

The mandate derives from the priorities established in relevant Security Council resolutions, including 1820 (2008), 1888 (2009), 1960 (2010), 2106 (2013) and 2467 (2019), as well as relevant country-specific and sanctions resolutions that make explicit reference to sexual violence in conflict and the mandate of the Special Representative. Furthermore, the adoption of Council resolutions 2331 (2016) and 2388 (2017) extends the scope of work of the Office to the areas of counter-terrorism, anti-trafficking efforts and related security and justice sector engagement.
Programme of work
Objective

The objective, to which the Office contributes, is to prevent and eradicate sexual violence as a tactic of war and terrorism and improve the provision of multisectoral services for survivors and the delivery of justice and accountability for such crimes.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the Office will continue to:

Monitor and report on sexual violence in conflict to the United Nations Security Council and other relevant United Nations bodies, including by establishing monitoring, analysis and reporting arrangements to compile updates from situations of concern;

Provide coherent and strategic leadership for the United Nations system on addressing conflict-related sexual violence, including through the United Nations Action against Sexual Violence in Conflict network to enhance prevention, service provision and system-wide coordination and response, and through the United Nations Team of Experts on the Rule of Law and Sexual Violence in Conflict to assist national authorities in strengthening the rule of law to ensure accountability for perpetrators of conflict-related sexual violence;

Engage in advocacy, on behalf of the United Nations system including through direct dialogue and/or country visits by the Special Representative, with governments, military and judicial representatives, as well as directly with parties to armed conflict on addressing conflict-related sexual violence, with a priority focus on justice and accountability as a key element of deterrence and prevention;

Support efforts at the country-level to prevent and respond to conflict-related sexual violence, including through the deployment of and support to Women Protection Advisers to situations of conflict, with a particular focus on mission transition contexts and non-mission settings, as well as the development of action plans, curricula and provision of training for national defence and security forces;

Encourage the United Nations sanctions committees to incorporate sexual violence considerations into their programmes of work pursuant to Security Council resolutions 1960(3) (2010); 2106(13) (2012); 2331 (2016); and 2467 (2019).

Enhance data analysis and information management capacity of the United Nations system to better capture the differentiated protection needs of survivors of conflict-related sexual violence, and factors that can exacerbate their vulnerability;

Adopt and promote a survivor-centred approach in the implementation of all aspects of the mandate, in coordination with survivors of sexual violence, survivors’ networks, civil society, regional organizations and relevant United Nations entities, in particular at the country level.
In doing so, the Office will support Member States to make progress towards the achievement of Sustainable Development Goals 5 and 16.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:

Adoption of concrete and time-bound commitments to prevent and address incidents, patterns and trends of conflict-related sexual violence, and accelerated implementation of existing political and operational agreements with affected States, including through increased measures taken by parties to armed conflict to prevent and protect against conflict-related sexual violence;

Increased access to survivor-centred justice, accountability and reparations for all survivors of conflict-related sexual violence, strengthened capacity of rule of law institutions and accountability mechanisms to deliver justice for CRSV at national level, increased number of national legislations related to conflict-related sexual violence aligned with international standards and best practices;
Improved access to holistic services, including medical care, psychosocial support, and livelihood support for all survivors, as well as for children born of conflict-related sexual violence;

Security Council and other relevant bodies have access to timely and reliable United Nations verified reporting and analysis on trends and patterns of violations and response to conflict-related sexual violence;
Increased capacity, coherence and coordination of the United Nations to prevent and respond to conflict-related sexual violence in line with a survivor-centered and trauma-informed approach;

Increased political consensus in multilateral and national settings that conflict-related sexual violence, in line with United Nations Security Council resolutions, should be addressed in peace, ceasefire, and other conflict-resolution processes and that survivors should have a role in these processes.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:

Continued high level of political will on the part of all stakeholders, in particular Member States, to work towards preventing and responding to sexual violence and ending the impunity of persistent perpetrators in situations of armed conflict and other situations of concern;

Member States and other key stakeholders see a convergence between their strategic interests and priorities and upholding the international protection framework that has been established to prevent and address conflict-related sexual violence;
The dynamics of armed conflict allow for access to monitor and assist in the implementation of political commitments to prevent and respond to conflict-related sexual violence;
Adequate extrabudgetary resources continue to be available to support delivery of the mandate.

With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, the Office will sustain its engagement with regional and subregional actors and multilateral institutions, including the African Union, the League of Arab States, the European Union, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, the Economic Community of West African States, the International Conference on the Great Lakes Region, the International Organization of la Francophonie, the Inter-Parliamentary Union and the African Development Bank.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Office will continue to work through the inter-agency network, United Nations Action against Sexual Violence in Conflict, a coalition of 27 United Nations entities, which is chaired by the Special Representative. The network will continue to provide strategic advocacy, knowledge generation, capacity building, coordination, and catalytic country-level support, guided by the recent system-wide needs assessment of the monitoring, analysis and reporting arrangements on conflict-related sexual violence, including through the formulation and dissemination of joint advocacy products to call upon the international community to provide political and financial support for survivors in situations of conflict and the development of new resources and technical guidance on emerging issues. Advocacy, coordination and the delivery of expert advice and assistance on justice and accountability dimensions of the mandate will continue to be conducted through the Team of Experts on the Rule of Law and Sexual Violence in Conflict, which operates under the strategic direction of the Special Representative, and comprises the Office, OHCHR, the United Nations Development Programme and the Department of Peace Operations as the co-lead entities. In addition, the Office will continue to strengthen its cooperation with, inter alia, the Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Children and Armed Conflict, the Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Violence against Children, the United Nations Global Counter-Terrorism Coordination Compact, the United Nations Resident Coordinator System and the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs and the Department of Peace Operations through periodic coordination meetings and information-sharing, to inform joint advocacy and operational strategies related to the prevention of and response to conflict-related sexual violence.

The Office integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate. Given the nature of the Office’s mandate, which is closely linked to the women and peace and security agenda, all its activities are ultimately aimed at promoting gender equality and women’s empowerment, as well as at addressing discrimination and harmful social norms that constitute invisible drivers of conflict-related sexual violence. As such, political commitments negotiated with parties to conflict (e.g., joint communiqués, frameworks of cooperation and implementation plans) will continue to integrate the views of women’s civil society organizations and will continue to promote the meaningful participation of women and girls in countries where they are often absent in political and decision-making processes, including peace processes. Prevention strategies, and response programming will reflect a tailored approach to address sexual violence against all survivors,. Information, including on incidents of conflict-related sexual violence, will continue to be systematically disaggregated by sex to allow for a gender-sensitive analysis and better inform action by the Security Council.

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the Office will continue to incorporate issues relating to disability inclusion into policy, advocacy, communications, and key substantive aspects of its work, including programming, monitoring and reporting in priority situations. The NGO-civil society advisory group of the Office includes entities representing individuals with disabilities and, through this modality, the Office will continue to engage with individuals with disabilities and with relevant organizations during the course of field missions in priority countries. The Office’s staff includes individuals with explicit human rights expertise relating to the rights of persons with disabilities, including those targeted with sexual violence in situations of concern.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects efforts of the programme to implement all mandates in a more efficient and effective manner and contains no substantive adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative.

The Office will be guided by any future decisions taken in the context of the UN80 Initiative, in accordance with the applicable rules and procedures, including decisions, resolutions and established practice of the competent intergovernmental organs.
Programme performance in 2025
Strengthened national ownership to prevent conflict-related sexual violence and deliver justice for survivors: the case of Ukraine

Since 2022, in response to allegations of conflict-related sexual violence in Ukraine, the Office led the development and implementation of a comprehensive victim-centered system-wide strategy to prevent and respond to conflict-related sexual violence in Ukraine. The early advocacy, mobilisation of United Nations entities and Member States political and financial support and the early deployment of specialised technical advice and expertise resulted in a unique pioneering model that brought together national authorities, the United Nations, survivor networks, and partner organizations. A framework of cooperation was signed between the Special Representative, on behalf of the United Nations system, and the government of Ukraine in May 2022. The Framework’s Implementation Plan was subsequently rapidly developed over a period of two months through extensive co-led consultations and comprehensive stakeholder participation as a unified roadmap across five priority areas: accountability, trafficking, services, reparations, and reform of the security sector. Through its advocacy, the Office mobilized Member States’ support and voluntary funding to deploy specialized expertise to operationalize commitments under the framework. This included the rapid deployment of: (i) specialized capacity to document and verify allegations, (ii) a Senior Women Protection Adviser to the office of the Resident Coordinator to support coordination and oversee the monitoring and reporting arrangements; (iii) specialized coordination and programmatic capacity to the United Nations Country Team; and (iv) international and national experts within key ministries to strengthen national capacity and support the implementation of the Framework’s commitments. The Team of Experts supported the development of a survivor-centered, trauma-informed strategy to national investigations and prosecutions, set up national specialized units, and delivered training, mentoring, and technical guidance. Since 2022, more than 650 prosecutors, investigators, judges, and legal aid providers built specialized skills, including in strategic case-building and trauma-informed interviewing, through scenario-based skills training. In addition, the United Nations Action against Sexual Violence in Conflict network spearheaded a catalytic project bringing together six United Nations entities that delivered multisectoral services to more than 2,200 survivors and supported the creation of Survivor Relief Centres across the country. In 2025, nationwide evaluations and consultations to assess progress on the implementation of the Framework were co-led by the Office with the Office of the Gender Commissioner and resulted in an updated implementation plan for 2026–2027.

text: VI.	Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Violence against Children

children.text: A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Violence against Children is responsible for mobilizing action and political support to prevent and eliminate all forms of violence against children. The mandate of the Office of the Special Representative derives from the priorities established in relevant General Assembly resolutions and decisions, including resolutions 62/141, 67/152, 73/155  78/187 and 80/190. While noting substantial progress achieved since establishing the mandate of the Special Representative, in renewing the mandate of the Special Representative for a further four-year period until 2029 the Assembly has recognized the urgency of pursuing further action to ensure the protection of children from violence. As of 2027, it is proposed that a single post will serve a dual role, concurrently comprising the responsibilities of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Violence against Children and the Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Children and Armed Conflict, with one incumbent heading the two distinct offices focused on their respective mandates.
Programme of work
Objective
The objective, to which the Office contributes, is to accelerate action to end all forms of violence against children by 2030.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the Office will:

(a)	Promote the acceleration of efforts towards the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals relating to addressing all forms and drivers of violence against children and gender-based violence by undertaking high-level advocacy at the global, regional and national levels in collaboration with key stakeholders;
(b)	Support Member States in the implementation of their pledges arising from the first Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence against Children;

(c)	Support Member States of the Pathfinding Global Alliance on Ending Violence against Children, noted by the General Assembly in its resolution 80/190 both as a contribution and accelerator of the prevention and protection of children against violence, in the implementation of their identified priority actions facilitating peer learning and knowledge-sharing among States;

(d)	Engage and support political, legislative, programmatic and monitoring processes at the global, regional, national and local levels to strengthen investment in child protection and well-being; conduct country visits in close cooperation with United Nations resident coordinators and regional or country teams; provide technical cooperation and practical guidance to Member States, including with respect to strengthening the collection of data on violence against children; share context-specific promising practices; enhance demand-driven bilateral and multilateral partnerships;

(e)	Increase the attention given to violence against children in the United Nations system, including through leading the Inter-Agency Working Group on Violence against Children and through advocacy for the system-wide mainstreaming of child rights, including the integration of child protection into United Nations programmatic tools, such as the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks;

(f)	Advocate, as Chair of the United Nations task force on children deprived of liberty, for the use of the detention of children to be only a measure of last resort; work towards prevention, rehabilitation and community-based alternatives to deprivation of liberty; and gather and report on promising practices regarding alternatives to detention and institutionalization;

(g)	Promote the role of children as agents of change through inclusive child participation in decision-making processes and the documentation and dissemination of child-led and peer-to-peer initiatives;
(h)	Promote investment in integrated, cross-sectoral child- and gender-sensitive protection and violence prevention;
(i)	Promote child protection as a cross-cutting theme in global, regional and national action to address trafficking in children.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:

(a)	Action to prevent and respond to violence against children mainstreamed into law, policy and programmes through costed intersectoral action plans supported by strong monitoring, coordination and information management systems;
(b)	Increased awareness of and action on key thematic and frontier issues requiring specific attention;
(c)	Sustained investment in cross-sectoral services for children and their caregivers to prevent and respond to violence against children and gender-based violence;
(d)	Adoption and effective implementation of prevention measures, rehabilitation and community-based alternatives to the deprivation of liberty of children;
(e)	More effective and systematic involvement of children in decision-making processes, including through an increase in safe and empowering pathways provided by States.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a)   Governments have the political commitment and dedicate resources to accelerate action to prevent and end violence against children, in the framework of the Sustainable Development Goals;
(b)	Civil society, faith-based organizations, local communities, the donor community and the private sector are committed to working together for and with children.

With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, the Office will continue to strengthen cooperation with intergovernmental regional and subregional bodies. The Office will continue to forge regular engagement with United Nations entities, State partners and others, including regional organizations, based away from New York, building on the strong liaison that it has established and ensuring stronger coherence around child protection and wellbeing frameworks. The Office will pursue strong collaboration with civil society and faith-based organizations and the private sector.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Office continues to promote and strengthen collaboration within the United Nations system on ending violence against children, including with the members of the Inter-Agency Working Group on Violence against Children, the members of the United Nations task force on children deprived of liberty, the Office of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Children and Armed Conflict, the Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Sexual Violence in Conflict, the special procedures of the Human Rights Council, the human rights treaty bodies, the Special Adviser to the Secretary-General on Africa, the United Nations Youth Office, the Office for Digital and Emerging Technologies, the Department of Economic and Social Affairs, United Nations resident coordinators and country team members.

The Office integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate, including in its advocacy to highlight how various forms of violence affect boys and girls differently and how this must inform and shape responses. Addressing gender discrimination and harmful social norms, as well as connections between violence against women and violence against children, is crucial to preventing and responding to violence against children and will continue to constitute an integral part of the Office’s work.

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy and the principle of leaving no child behind, the Office places an emphasis on addressing some of the most vulnerable and neglected children, among whom are children with disabilities. Promoting policies and strategies for alternative means of care will continue to be at the core of the Office’s advocacy. The Office will continue to pay particular attention to the inclusion of children with disabilities in all its consultations.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative
The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects efforts of the programme to implement all mandates in a more efficient and effective manner.

The Office will be guided by any future decisions taken in the context of the UN80 Initiative, in accordance with the applicable rules and procedures, including decisions, resolutions and established practice of the competent intergovernmental organs. This includes any decisions concerning the proposal for a single post to serve a dual role, concurrently comprising the responsibilities of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Violence against Children and the Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Children and Armed Conflict, as part of the review of thematic and geographic envoys.

Strengthened commitment of the private sector to protect children from violence in the context of travel and tourism

Many child protection challenges emerge in the context of travel and tourism, whether as a result of offenders moving within or between States, technology-facilitated abuse, or as an unintended result of the activities and operations of the sector itself. As the travel and tourism industry was rebuilding after the COVID-19 pandemic, the Special Representative determined that it was a strategic moment to re-engage the sector and put child protection at the core of its sustainability agenda. The Special Representative consequently focused her 2023 annual report to the General Assembly on this theme and re-engaged the industry. She supported the creation of a working group of the World Travel and Tourism Council, leading industry representatives and civil society to identify and share good practices and develop a joint advocacy strategy. Following sustained advocacy by the Special Representative, the World Travel and Tourism Council included child protection as an explicit priority in its social impact work at its annual meeting in October 2024. Another important milestone was the World Travel and Tourism Council Summit in September 2025, during which participating chief executive officers committed to incorporate child protection as a key dimension in their companies’ sustainability strategies.

The facilitation of peer learning between Member States is a key pillar of the Special Representative’s mandate. At the request of Member States, she led the development of a marketplace for knowledge-sharing on measures to end violence against children. Supported by the United Nations System Staff College, the marketplace is a platform where States and all key stakeholders can share expertise, have access to practical resources and connect with and learn from one another.
