text: VIII.	Office of the United Nations Special Coordinator on Improving the United Nations Response to Sexual Exploitation and Abuse

children.text: A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The Office was established in February 2016, when the Secretary-General appointed the Special Coordinator with a reporting line through the Chef de Cabinet to the Secretary-General to work across the United Nations system’s offices, departments and agencies to strengthen the United Nations response to sexual exploitation and abuse, wherever it might occur, from headquarters locations to the most remote field bases. The General Assembly, in its resolution 70/286, and the Security Council, by its resolution 2272 (2016), welcomed the appointment of the Special Coordinator and the Secretary-General’s continued efforts to implement and reinforce the United Nations zero-tolerance policy on sexual exploitation and abuse, in particular to strengthen the Organization’s prevention, reporting, enforcement and remedial action in order to promote greater accountability. In its resolution 71/278, the Assembly welcomed the continued efforts of the Secretary-General to combat sexual exploitation and abuse, including the appointment of a Special Coordinator on improving the United Nations response to sexual exploitation and abuse and the establishment of a high-level task force to develop, as a matter of urgency, a clear, game-changing strategy to achieve visible and measurable improvements in the Organization’s approach to preventing and responding to sexual exploitation and abuse. The Assembly also expressed its support to the Secretary-General, the Office and all relevant departments in their efforts to implement the zero-tolerance policy and, in particular, to strengthen the Organization’s prevention, reporting, enforcement and response mechanisms in order to promote greater accountability, and in that regard requested the Secretary-General to continue to work in close consultation with Member States for the effective implementation of the policy.

The Special Coordinator drives and oversees United Nations efforts to prevent and respond to sexual exploitation and abuse across the United Nations system. Through the development of procedures, protocols, standardized tools and support for United Nations entities at Headquarters and in the field, the Special Coordinator continues efforts to align approaches and enhance coordination, cooperation and system-wide coherence.
Programme of work
Objective

The objective, to which the Office contributes, is to advance the United Nations response to sexual exploitation and abuse and to ensure a continuous focus on and sustained high-level attention to the prevention and response to sexual exploitation and abuse through a victim-centred approach.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the Office will:

(a)	Coordinate with United Nations entities, departments and offices to ensure the alignment and institutionalization of strategies to prevent and respond to sexual exploitation and abuse by developing initiatives to mitigate the risks of sexual exploitation and abuse across the United Nations system;

(b)	Promote the implementation of the Secretary-General’s strategy to combat sexual exploitation and abuse across the system’s more than 30 affiliated funds, programmes and specialized agencies and act as the secretariat of the Secretary-General’s institutionalized standing bodies for protection against sexual exploitation and abuse, such as the High-level Steering Group on preventing sexual exploitation and abuse, convened by the Chef de Cabinet, which oversees the implementation of the Secretary-General’s strategy;

(c)	Guide organization-wide change management to implement the updated Secretary-General’s Bulletin on sexual exploitation and abuse across all categories of United Nations personnel, both uniformed and civilian, and non-United Nations actors;

(d)	Consult with international, regional and subregional organizations, Member States, United Nations independent human rights experts, civil society organizations, national human rights institutions, academic institutions and think tanks, as appropriate, to ensure that policies and operational efforts across the United Nations system reflect best practice;
(e)	Monitor and enhance the Secretary-General’s public reporting mechanism for allegations of sexual exploitation and abuse;

(f)	Strengthen accountability and transparency through a multifaceted approach which engages leadership across Member States and within the United Nations system, reinforces commitment, processes and engagement at the national level, fosters collaboration with Member States, augments investigative capacity, strengthens legislative frameworks and ensure a victim-centred, trauma-informed approach;

(g)	Work closely with managers at all levels across the United Nations system to provide strategic support and guidance, and strengthen leadership capacity through advocacy, policy development and practical learning.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:

(a)	Strengthened prevention of and responses to sexual exploitation and abuse in a coherent and coordinated manner, including improved awareness, risk mitigation, data collection, evidence-based interventions, monitoring and analysis of performance and improved victim support and assistance by the United Nations system;

(b)	Institutionalization of an organizational culture that prohibits sexual exploitation and abuse and inaction to same, with a robust and consistent understanding among United Nations personnel of standards of conduct and the purpose of mission of the United Nations, to advance cultural change and address the underpinnings of sexual exploitation and abuse, including gender imbalances and the abuse of authority due to power differentials.
With regard to external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a)	Personnel, at all levels, prioritize combating sexual exploitation and abuse within United Nations operations;
(b) 	Adequate resources are available to support delivery of the mandate;
(c)	The United Nations system supports the alignment and institutionalization of measures to prevent and respond to sexual exploitation and abuse, including through sustained, predictable funding.

With regard to inter-agency coordination, the Office will continue to seek cooperation with all United Nations partners, including agencies, funds and programmes, and the Inter-Agency Standing Committee and its Champion on protection from sexual exploitation and abuse and sexual harassment, to ensure coordination with relevant mandates and a coherent and consistent response. The Office will also continue to collaborate with the Office of the Victims’ Rights Advocate, the Department of Management Strategy, Policy and Compliance and the Department of Global Communications, among other entities within the Organization, to ensure alignment of messages relating to the prevention of and response to sexual exploitation and abuse in internal and external communications. Furthermore, the Office will work closely with the Development Coordination Office and resident coordinators, globally, to support their roles and responsibilities in accordance with the management and accountability framework of the United Nations development and resident coordinator system. The Office continues to serve as the secretariat of the Secretary-General’s circle of leadership on the prevention of and response to sexual exploitation and abuse in United Nations operations, which comprises global leaders who actively support the agenda of combating sexual exploitation and abuse.

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the Office will identify ways to ensure the integration of disability inclusion across all programs and interventions. This involves mainstreaming disability inclusion through training and outreach material on preventing and responding to sexual exploitation and abuse, including on victim support, that is tailored to address the distinct needs and challenges of individuals with disabilities.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects changes arising from the UN80 Initiative, in particular, the tables of deliverables reflect updated deliverables for 2026, in line with the approved programme budget for 2026.

The Office will be guided by any future decisions taken in the context of the UN80 Initiative, in accordance with the applicable rules and procedures, including decisions, resolutions and established practice of the competent intergovernmental organs.
Evaluation activities
The following evaluations completed in 2025 have guided the proposed programme plan for 2027:
Review of policies and practices to prevent and respond to sexual exploitation and abuse in the United Nations system organizations conducted by the Joint Inspection Unit (JIU/REP/2025/2).
Comprehensive Assessment of Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse commissioned by the Office.

In response to the results of the evaluations referenced above, the Office will work towards establishing a coordinated approach across the United Nations system to prevent and respond to sexual exploitation and abuse through an updated system-wide strategy and a five-year implementation plan. Key areas of focus will include aligning policies, definitions, and approaches on emerging issues, including technology-facilitated sexual exploitation and abuse, to ensure coherence across all entities and address gaps identified by the evaluations. The Office will also ensure harmonized data collection and reporting standards across the system. In addition, efforts will focus on strengthening system-wide vetting and screening procedures through standardized tools and harmonized implementation protocols and strengthening the accountability framework by assessing and updating disciplinary measures, procedural steps, and processes related to criminal referrals. The Office will further support system-wide efforts to promote a consistent victim-centred approach grounded in dignity, informed choice, and meaningful access.
Programme performance in 2025
Expanded Integration of Protection Measures in Country Cooperation Frameworks

Sexual exploitation and abuse are inherent risks across all United Nations system entities, regardless of context. In 2025, the Office worked with relevant actors to help ensure that those served by, and serving alongside, United Nations personnel can trust the Organization and remain safe. To support this effort, the Office further strengthened its strategic role in key coordination forums, enhanced outreach initiatives, and deepened collaboration with both internal and external stakeholders, including government counterparts to reinforce common standards.  This included continued advocacy for the integration of a model clause on protection from sexual exploitation and abuse in United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks, as part of broader efforts to promote joint action, build national capacity and mainstream protection into government systems.

children.text: Result 3: Strengthened system-wide strategic approach to addressing sexual exploitation and abuse – Proposed programme plan for 2027

Combating sexual exploitation and abuse demands system-wide commitment and action at all levels and across all pillars of the United Nations. The Office is working to develop a new system-wide strategy, which is anticipated to be launched in 2027. The new strategy is intended to strengthen policy coherence, expand comprehensive education for all personnel and deliver targeted capacity-building.
Lessons learned and planned change

The lesson for the Office was that meaningful and sustained change cannot be achieved through compliance exercises and normative measures alone but requires the continuous implementation of a deliberate and system-wide strategy that promotes cultural change, continuous learning and engagement across the UN system and its partners. In applying the lesson, the Office will continue to build momentum through an updated system-wide strategy that advances standards of conduct and policies on sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment; deepens leadership development to reinforce managerial responsibility and role-modelling of expected behaviours; and strengthens mechanisms to support consistent implementation across peacekeeping, humanitarian, and development contexts.

children.text: A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The Office of the United Nations Ombudsman and Mediation Services is responsible for providing confidential, impartial and independent conflict resolution services to address work-related issues of staff members and non-staff personnel, upon request. In doing so, the United Nations Ombudsman makes an essential contribution to making the Organization a productive, healthy and enabling workplace.

The mandate of the Office derives from the priorities established in relevant General Assembly resolutions and/or decisions, including resolutions 55/258 and 56/253. The Office was further strengthened by the Assembly, pursuant to its resolutions 61/261 and 62/228, to create an integrated and geographically decentralized Office. By its resolution 73/276, the Assembly requested the Secretary-General to establish, within existing resources, a pilot project to offer access to informal dispute resolution services to non-staff personnel. By its resolution 78/248, the Assembly decided to regularize the pilot project for access by non-staff personnel to the services of the Office, within existing resources.
Programme of work
Objective

The objective, to which this Office contributes, is to ensure the effective functioning of the Organization by enhancing harmony in the workplace through an efficient and effective option for staff and non-staff personnel to seek redress to grievances.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the Office will:

Provide the full range of conflict resolution services to United Nations staff and non-staff personnel in three core areas: addressing workplace grievances from staff and non-staff personnel through case intervention; engaging with relevant stakeholders to provide systemic feedback for improvements in the workplace; and strengthening, through capacity-building initiatives, the ability of staff and non-staff personnel to address workplace conflict effectively;

Strengthen the Organization’s informal conflict resolution system through enhanced accessibility, visibility, and effectiveness of services, focusing on outreach efforts to raise awareness of the importance of informal dispute resolution as a preferred first step.

Ensure that staff and non-staff personnel, irrespective of location, have access to the informal pillar of the administration of justice and to informal conflict resolution services, including by providing services in all six official languages of the United Nations;
Conduct regular presentations on “civility, communication and community,” in various languages to global offices to promote and facilitate healthy dialogue among colleagues.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:
A more harmonious and collaborative work environment for United Nations staff and non-staff personnel;
More productive and more effective functioning of the Organization;
Improved awareness among managers, staff and non-staff personnel of the importance of resilience and flexibility in fostering a harmonious workplace.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
All staff and non-staff personnel, including those in supervisory functions, avail themselves of opportunities to resolve workplace issues through established informal mechanisms;

All staff and non-staff personnel observe applicable United Nations regulations and rules regarding the terms and conditions of employment and apply lessons learned from decisions of the United Nations Dispute Tribunal and the United Nations Appeals Tribunal;

With regard to cooperation with other entities and inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Office will continue to build stronger collaboration with the formal system of administration of justice to explore opportunities for more referrals from the formal to the informal pillar. The Office will also continue to cooperate with the network of ombudsmen and mediators of the United Nations system so as to contribute to improved system-wide cohesion and impact in the area of conflict resolution in the workplace.

The Office integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results as appropriate. This includes gender considerations in the delivery of conflict resolution services and in the identification of systemic issues, including feedback on gender-related inequities observed in cases presented to the Office. The Office will also continue to support the implementation of the strategy included in the system-wide policy on gender equality and the empowerment of women. The Office also compiles gender-disaggregated data.

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the Office will take into account the needs of persons with disabilities and facilitate their full and effective participation in its activities. In collaboration with the Department of Global Communications, the Office will maintain accessibility features on its website and online platforms to support users with temporary or long-term disabilities.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects efforts of the Office to implement all mandates in a more efficient and effective manner and contains no substantive adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative.

The Office will be guided by any future decisions taken in the context of the UN80 Initiative, in accordance with the applicable rules and procedures, including decisions, resolutions and established practice of the competent intergovernmental organs.
Evaluation activities
The following evaluation completed in 2025 has guided the proposed programme plan for 2027:
Evaluation conducted by the Office on client satisfaction

In response to the results of the evaluation referenced above, the Office will promote the early use of mediation through targeted outreach and engagement with stakeholders to identify opportunities for piloting early referrals. Where possible, the Office will also offer additional conflict competence skill-building workshops for staff and non-staff personnel to equip them with practical tools to help prevent or constructively address workplace conflicts, including managing difficult conversations, giving and receiving feedback, and fostering a harmonious workplace.
An evaluation on client satisfaction, to be conducted by the Office, is planned for 2027.
Programme performance in 2025
Managing workplace conflict better through capacity- and skill-building activities

The principle of dignity is a cornerstone of the Organization, as reaffirmed in the Staff Regulations and Rules of the United Nations, in which it is stated that “staff members shall uphold and respect the principles set out in the Charter, including faith in fundamental human rights, in the dignity and worth of the human person and in the equal rights of men and women”. In its systemic observations, the Office has consistently highlighted concerns related to issues of dignity and respect and has pointed out the impact of such issues on team climate and morale, stressing the need to foster an inclusive and respectful work environment.  In 2025, the Office organized workshops on civility, communication and community, focusing on the connection between dignity, communication and civility in the workplace, and enabling participants to reflect on how their interactions can enhance or undermine dignity.
Progress towards the objective is presented in the performance measure below (see figure 1.XXI).
Performance measure: number of personnel equipped to manage workplace conflict
Planned results for 2027
Result 1: United Nations non-staff personnel have access to informal conflict resolution services – Programme performance in 2025 and target for 2027
The Office’s work contributed to 265 non-staff personnel utilizing informal conflict resolution services, which exceeded the planned target of 200.
Progress towards the objective and the target for 2027 are presented in the performance measure below (see figure 1.XXII).
Performance measure: number of non-staff personnel using informal conflict resolution services (annual)
Result 2: increased access of services for staff in the field – Programme performance in 2025 and target for 2027

The Office’s work contributed to 750 informal conflict services accessed by staff in the field, which did not meet the planned target of 800.  The target was not met primarily due to financial constraints that limited the office’s ability to conduct in-person visits, particularly to hardship duty stations and remote locations.
Progress towards the objective and the target for 2027 are presented in the performance measure below (see figure 1.XXIII).
Performance measure: number of informal conflict services accessed by staff in the field (annual)
Result 3: Improved awareness of mediation services – Proposed programme plan for 2027

The Office, through its mediation services provides a structured, collaborative process to manage and help to resolve workplace disputes, conflicts, concerns, and differences with the assistance of an impartial third party. This approach is most useful when parties are looking to resolve a specific, identified issue. The Office conducts information sessions about understanding the benefits and added value of workplace mediations as the “informal first approach” to conflict resolution in the Organization.
Lessons learned and planned change

The lesson for the Office was that there was a lack of awareness and knowledge among staff and managers of the benefits of mediation as a constructive and accessible approach to resolving workplace conflicts. In applying the lesson, the Office will seek to increase awareness of mediation and conduct additional sessions in various languages to reach United Nations personnel globally.
Expected progress towards the objective is presented in the performance measure below (see figure 1. XXIV).

children.text: A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The Office of Administration of Justice is responsible for the overall coordination of the system of administration of justice and contributing to its functioning in a fair, transparent and efficient manner. The mandate of the Office derives from relevant General Assembly resolutions, including resolutions 61/261, 62/228 and 63/253, by which the Assembly established a new, independent, transparent, professionalized, adequately resourced and decentralized system of administration of justice and placed emphasis on the need to ensure the fair and just treatment of United Nations staff and the accountability of managers and staff alike.
Programme of work
Objective

The objective, to which the Office contributes, is to ensure access to justice, respect for the rights and obligations of staff members and the accountability of managers and staff members alike through the efficient and effective functioning of the system of administration of justice.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the Office will:

(a)	Provide easy access to jurisprudence through the website of the United Nations system of administration of justice, the fully searchable jurisprudence database accessible via the case law portal, and outreach means;
(b)	Provide legal advice and assistance and, where appropriate, legal representation to staff;
(c)	Enhance the case management systems and procedures and provide substantive, technical and administrative support to the United Nations Dispute Tribunal and the United Nations Appeals Tribunal;
(d)	Raise awareness of and increase access to workplace dispute resolution mechanisms, with a focus on field missions and offices.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:
(a)	Improved decision-making by managers;
(b)	Increased access to information on when and how to pursue a claim before the Tribunals;
(c)	Effective dispute resolution;
(d)	More expedient processing of cases.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a)	Staff members avail themselves of opportunities to resolve workplace disputes through established informal mechanisms;

(b)	Staff members observe applicable United Nations regulations and rules regarding the terms and conditions of employment and apply lessons learned from decisions of the Tribunals prior to filing applications;
(c)	Caseload and disposal of cases remain stable;
(d)	Staff members in remote locations have Internet connectivity to file electronically.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Office will continue to implement its comprehensive outreach strategy to provide staff with improved access to information and resources to resolve workplace grievances. To continue to implement this strategy and reach out to the largest number of staff members possible, particularly in locations away from Headquarters, the Office will work collaboratively with several entities and the separately administered funds and programmes. In 2027, the Office will continue to invest in promoting outreach activities to raise awareness of the case law portal, including in cooperation with other agencies. The Office will also continue to coordinate the preparation of the report of the Secretary-General on the functioning of the system of administration of justice and report on trends and observations.

The Office integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate. The Office will continue to identify any systemic issues concerning gender inequality in the access to the system of administration of justice and recommend remedial action. The Office’s gender team will continue to support the implementation of the system-wide policy on gender equality and the empowerment of women.

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the Office will maintain accessibility features on the website of the Office that benefit users with temporary or long-term disabilities, in collaboration with the Department of Global Communications.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects efforts of the Office to implement all mandates in a more efficient and effective manner and contains no substantive adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative.

The Office will be guided by any future decisions taken in the context of the UN80 Initiative, in accordance with the applicable rules and procedures, including decisions, resolutions and established practice of the competent intergovernmental organs.

This enhancement provides greater clarity to applicants and other stakeholders on the status and progression of cases. It also supports more timely processing of cases by providing key stakeholders with greater visibility of caseload distribution, thereby enabling more effective planning.

Performance measure: number of legal assistance requests from staff members received by the Office of Staff Legal Assistance (annual) – Result 3:  More timely resolution of cases before the United Nations Dispute Tribunal – Proposed programme plan for 2027

Cases before the United Nations Dispute Tribunal are assigned to judges, with the General Assembly establishing a 90-day deadline for first judicial action and a 400-day deadline for the disposition of each case. In order to support timely and efficient dispute resolution, it is important that cases are assigned to judges by the registries without delay following submission. Previously, cases were held for assignment until a judge was available, which could delay the commencement of active judicial case management. The Office has begun systematically assigning cases to duty judges, judges rostered to receive and manage newly filed cases, within a short time frame, as appropriate, after a case has been filed. This measure facilitates timely case management by judges, enabling cases to progress towards hearings or closing submissions and disposal, and contributing to a reduction in overall case processing timelines.
Lessons learned and planned change

The lesson for the Office was that prompt case assignment to duty judges and earlier judicial case management contributes to timely case disposal. In applying the lesson, all new cases will be assigned to duty judges within a short time frame, as appropriate, after a case has been filed.

text: XI.	Ethics Office

children.text: A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The Ethics Office was established as an independent Secretariat office and is responsible for assisting the Secretary-General in ensuring that all staff members perform their functions consistent with the highest standards of integrity, as required under the Charter of the United Nations. The mandate of the Office derives from the priorities established in relevant General Assembly resolutions and/or decisions, including resolutions 60/1 and 60/248. The Office also assists the Secretary-General in reporting annually to the Assembly on the implementation of ethics policies in response to Assembly resolution 60/254 and on the activities of the Ethics Panel of the United Nations pursuant to Assembly resolution 63/250. Pursuant to Assembly resolution 77/278, the Office directly presents an annual report to the Assembly. Further to Assembly resolution 70/305, the Office has been mandated to participate in providing an induction briefing to all Presidents of the General Assembly and their offices, to review the financial disclosures of those Presidents and to vet all private contributions to the Office of the President of the General Assembly. As provided for in Assembly resolution 71/263, the Office aims to do its part in the swift and effective implementation of the revised policy on protection against retaliation and to cultivate an organizational culture in which staff feel free to speak up.
Programme of work
Objective

The objective, to which the Office contributes, is to achieve and sustain an organizational culture of integrity, accountability and transparency, wherein all staff members observe and perform their functions consistent with the highest standards of integrity required under the Charter of the United Nations.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the Office will:

(a)	Provide independent and preventive ethics advice, guidance and briefings to staff and management to ensure that ethical standards are well understood, support ethics standard-setting and promote policy coherence within the Secretariat and among the Organization’s separately administered organs and programmes;

(b)	Deliver its services in line with its terms of reference outlined in the relevant Secretary-General’s bulletins (ST/SGB/2005/22, ST/SGB/2007/11 and ST/SGB/2007/11/Amend.1), through the administration of the annual financial disclosure programme, the provision of guidance and confidential ethics advice (including pre-appointment disclosure reviews for senior appointments and through the ethics helpline), the conduct of ethics briefings and outreach, and the fulfilment of the Office’s responsibilities regarding the protection against retaliation policy, and by ensuring policy support and coherence of ethical standards;
(c)	Identify risks in staff engagement in outside activities, in particular in terms of potential conflicts of interest and their impact on the Organization;
(d)	Foster a shared understanding of the standards of conduct for the international civil service through the Ethics Network of Multilateral Organizations member entities affiliated with CEB;

(e)	Support the Organization’s overall strategy on risk management, including identifying and mitigating personal and organizational conflicts of interest through the financial disclosure programme and the provision of advice, and, upon request, work with the various owners of the risks identified in the enterprise risk registry in updating and implementing their response plans;

(f)	Communicate and demonstrate the availability of measures for protection against retaliation, by continuously working within the Secretariat (with the Department of Global Communications, OIOS and the Department of Management Strategy, Policy and Compliance) and throughout the United Nations system through outreach activities.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:

(a)	Greater public trust in the integrity of the Organization through the financial disclosure exercise, retaining the foundational defence for the Organization from personal conflicts of interest and potential reputational damage;
(b)	Awareness among a greater number of staff of ethical standards and practices and of provisions for protection against retaliation;
(c)	Enhanced organizational culture of integrity, transparency and accountability.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a)	Staff continue to avail themselves of the services provided by the Office;
(b)	Financial disclosure statements from staff are submitted to the Office in a timely manner;
(c)	All necessary documentation is provided by staff when seeking protection against retaliation;
(d)	The security and public health situations in duty stations will allow for in-person outreach missions, when required.

With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, the Office expects to participate in the annual meeting of the Ethics Network of Multilateral Organizations.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Director of the Office will continue to chair and provide functional leadership to the Ethics Panel to increase coherence in the work of member ethics offices, as reflected in Secretary-General’s bulletins ST/SGB/2007/11 and ST/SGB/2007/11/Amend.1. The Office will continue to engage with the Ethics Network of Multilateral Organizations member entities affiliated with CEB in the interest of ethics policy coherence and to promote protection against retaliation in the United Nations system. It will also continue to administer the financial disclosure requirements of those system entities that have opted to outsource this requirement to the Secretariat’s Ethics Office. It will further continue to review contested matters by the staff of the separately administered organs and programmes of the Ethics Panel.

The Office integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate. It disaggregates its service data by gender, where possible. The Office has received more enquiries from women consistently over the years and has responded to them. As a practice, and when funds allow, outreach mission teams of the Office will continue to be in pairs and gender-balanced. Subject to demand from requesting entities, the Office will provide gender-disaggregated information.

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the Office will take into account the needs of persons with disabilities and facilitate their full and effective participation in its activities.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects efforts of the Office to implement all mandates in a more efficient and effective manner and contains no substantive adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative.

The Office will be guided by any future decisions taken in the context of the UN80 Initiative, in accordance with the applicable rules and procedures, including decisions, resolutions and established practice of the competent intergovernmental organs.
Evaluation activities
The Office plans to conduct an internal evaluation in 2027 on a topic to be determined.
Programme performance in 2025
Increased staff confidence in seeking advice on protection against retaliation

Ensuring that misconduct can be reported without fear of retaliation is essential for fostering integrity, transparency, and accountability across the Organization. The Office provides confidential advice, guidance and education on ethics-related matters, including issues concerning protection against retaliation. Over the years, the Office has observed a steady rise in requests related to protection against retaliation, especially requests for advice and preliminary reviews. These trends reflect several factors: the increasing  complexity of operational environments; heightened global expectations around compliance and accountability; and shifts and uncertainty in staff work situations, which can be attributed to the ongoing management initiatives and resulting structural changes within the Organization. Early interventions, aimed at addressing concerns, preventing risks of retaliation, and redressing instances of retaliation, are critical for maintaining and strengthening trust among staff in the accountability framework of the Organization, and safeguarding its credibility. In 2025, the Office responded to 177 advice queries on retaliation, compared with 134 in 2024, reflecting an increase of 32 per cent and a continued upward trend since 2021. This sustained rise reflects growing staff confidence in seeking confidential advice and engaging with the Organization’s misconduct reporting framework at an early stage. Through targeted outreach aimed at strengthening staff knowledge of, and trust in, the Organization’s policy on protection against retaliation, the Office has supported staff in understanding and gaining confidence in the Organization’s misconduct reporting channels, contributing to a culture grounded in ethics, transparency, and accountability.

A trusted system in which personnel can report misconduct, wrongdoing, or ethical concerns without fear of retaliation is a cornerstone of a strong culture of speaking up. Effective implementation of the protection against retaliation policy encourages staff to report concerns and enables the Organization to identify and mitigate risks in a timely manner. The Office has strengthened staff awareness of the policy through its enhanced advisory services and by ensuring adherence to policy deadlines in handling protection against retaliation matters, which helps instil trust in the effectiveness of the policy and the protection of whistleblowers.
Lessons learned and planned change

The lesson for the Office was that increased staff understanding of the protection against retaliation policy, combined with the timely processing of complaints, reinforces trust in the effectiveness of the policy. In applying the lesson, the Office will strengthen its approach to enhancing staff understanding of the policy through more targeted training and advisory services. text: XIII.	Resident coordinator system

children.text: A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

General Assembly resolution 72/279 on the repositioning of the United Nations development system and the Economic and Social Council segment on operational activities for development guide the scope and implementation of the activities of the resident coordinator system. In line with resolutions 72/279, 75/233, 79/226 and other relevant Assembly resolutions, the substantive mandates of the resident coordinator system are oriented around supporting countries in the implementation of the 2030 Agenda. The management of the resident coordinator system rests with the Development Coordination Office under the oversight of the Chair of the United Nations Sustainable Development Group, with resident coordinators reporting directly to the Secretary-General. Resident coordinators are the designated representatives of the Secretary-General for development coordination at the country level. At the heart of the resident coordinator system are 130 resident coordinators leading 130 United Nations country teams operating in over 160 countries and territories.
Programme of work
Objective

The objective, to which the resident coordinator system contributes, is to accelerate Member States’ progress towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals through leadership of the strengthened United Nations development support, robust coordination mechanisms, tools and frameworks, the effective management of joint resources and improved transparency of results to improve the impact, efficiency and effectiveness of operational activities for development at the country, regional and global levels.
Strategy and external factors for 2027

To contribute to the objective, the resident coordinator system will scale up development support to national Governments in order to implement the 2030 Agenda, including by strengthening the design and implementation of United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks. Specifically, the resident coordinator system will:
(a)	Ensure diverse and effective resident coordinator profiles and skill sets tailored to the needs of countries;

(b)	Provide effective support, through the Development Coordination Office, at the global and regional levels, to United Nations country teams in delivering individual and collective results on the Sustainable Development Goals, with the Resident Coordinator serving as the gateway to the United Nations’ collective offer for Member States;
(c)	Act as the secretariat for the United Nations Sustainable Development Group;
(d)	Ensure accountable and transparent results of the resident coordinator system and United Nations development system in support of the 2030 Agenda at the global, regional and national levels;

(e)	Support high-quality Sustainable Development Goal analysis and tailored responses by United Nations entities and governments at the country level, by leveraging data-driven solutions, information technology and digital innovation;

(f)	Facilitate the achievement of system-wide efficiencies of the United Nations Sustainable Development Group through the following workstreams: business operations strategies, common back offices, global shared services and common premises;

(g)	Continue to leverage catalytic funding provided by the Joint Sustainable Development Goals Fund to help countries to accelerate the achievement of the Goals by propelling key transitions in areas such as digitalization, food systems, energy, and social protection and jobs, with an emphasis on the localization of and synergies to be achieved across multiple Goals and fostering systems-level change for the 2030 Agenda;

(h)	In line with intergovernmental mandates, support Member States in addressing and proactively managing risks and taking steps to address and prevent crises. This approach will be anchored firmly within the United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:
(a)	A stronger convening role of United Nations development stakeholders to offer countries in-depth policy solutions to advance the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals;

(b)	A coherent and transparent approach to United Nations sustainable development operations at the national, regional and global levels, including consistent implementation of system-wide priorities, policies and approaches across United Nations Sustainable Development Group entities;

(c)	Strengthened partnerships to support Member States in their efforts to accelerate progress towards attaining the Sustainable Development Goals, including by attracting and leveraging public and private financing for the Goals;

(d)	Increased financial resources and effectiveness for United Nations programme implementation by reducing costs through the implementation of efficiency measures and by enhancing the agility of United Nations development activities;

(e)	The safeguarding of lives and livelihoods by continuing to address the socioeconomic and long-term impacts of multiple and interlocking crises whilst protecting and advancing progress on sustainable development.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a)	Adequate funding for the resident coordinator system, as well as for the Joint Sustainable Development Goals Fund and other key pooled funds;

(b)	Continued and renewed engagement by Member States on the funding compact and the implementation of related commitments to ensure that the quality and quantity of funding allows the United Nations development system to maximize its comparative advantages and further incentivize United Nations coherence.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the resident coordinator system will continue to actively coordinate member United Nations entities at the principal, director and technical levels. The resident coordinator system will also work closely with United Nations development entities and Secretariat entities, including peacekeeping and special political missions. The resident coordinators will continue to lead United Nations country teams in supporting national plans and priorities.

With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, the resident coordinator system will continue to work closely with Member States, international financial institutions and civil society partners to advance the Sustainable Development Goals and the 2030 Agenda.

The resident coordinator system integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate. The resident coordinator system will continue to enhance implementation of and reporting on the United Nations accountability framework on gender equality. For example, through the United Nations System-wide Gender Equality Acceleration Plan, the system will ensure the application of the United Nations country team gender equality marker to track planned investment by the country teams for gender equality and the empowerment of women and to advance gender-responsive realization of the Sustainable Development Goals.

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the resident coordinator system will focus on the implementation of the Strategy and support United Nations country teams in implementing and reporting on the Strategy; in parallel, the system will continue supporting programme country Governments to implement the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects efforts of the programme to implement all mandates in a more efficient and effective manner and contains no substantive adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative.

The resident coordinator system will be guided by any future decisions taken in the context of the UN80 Initiative, in accordance with the applicable rules and procedures, including decisions, resolutions and established practice of the competent intergovernmental organs. This includes, among others, any decisions concerning proposals related to the regional reset for sustainable development and the creation of regional integrated platforms, and those related to reconfiguring country-level support through cross-pillar delivery; as well as proposals related to the review of funding mechanisms, including proposals outlined in the report on the financing of and governance of the resident coordinator system, as requested by the General Assembly in its resolution 79/258 and to be considered by the Assembly during at its eighty-first session.
Evaluation activities
The following evaluations completed in 2025 have guided the proposed programme plan for 2027:
United Nations Sustainable Development Group system-wide evaluation of the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy;
United Nations Sustainable Development Group system-wide evaluation on progress towards a “new generation of United Nations country teams”;
OIOS evaluation of the Resident Coordinator system support for graduation in least developed countries;
20 United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks evaluations.

In response to the findings and recommendations of the system-wide evaluations referenced above, the Development Coordination Office operationalised recommendation 2.5 of the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy system-wide evaluation, which calls for Resident Coordinators to convene United Nations country teams to develop, implement, and monitor disability inclusion action Plans aligned with the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. This included providing dedicated technical support through a toolkit and concise guidance notes, as well as the consolidation of good practices from country and regional implementation to promote more consistent system-wide practice. In line with the agreed management response to the evaluation on a new generation of United Nations country teams, DCO launched a revision of the Cooperation Framework guidance, expected to be finalized in the third quarter of 2026. Furthermore, in response to the OIOS evaluation, DCO will deepen its support to the Resident Coordinators Offices in least developed countries to enhance integration of the Doha Programme of Action by the United Nations country teams in United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks.  Findings from the evaluations of United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks are being implemented by relevant United Nations country teams, including to strengthen planning and implementation structures and mechanisms, enhance monitoring, evaluation and data collection systems, increase stakeholder engagement and improve alignment with national priorities.

23 United Nations Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks evaluations are planned for 2027, namely 11 in the Africa region, 5 in the Asia and Pacific region, 5 in the Latin America and the Caribbean region, and 2 in the Europe and Central Asia region.
Programme performance in 2025
National Governments advanced integrated policy approaches to Sustainable Development Goal acceleration

Resident coordinators lead United Nations system-wide support to host governments in ensuring integrated policy formulation at the national level to advance progress across the SDGs. In 2025, resident coordinators worked with host Governments to support their preparations of the new Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement, ahead of the 30th Conference of Parties of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP30). Resident coordinators supported 107 host Governments in the formulation effort of the NDCs, helping ensure the adoption of an economy-wide approach to support SDG acceleration synergistically with climate action. Through their convening leadership, resident coordinators harnessed the expertise of 30 United Nations entities to support Governments in this effort, helping ensure that new NDCs act as vehicles for integrated policies and financing spanning key sectors and SDGs such as agriculture and food systems (SDG2), energy (SDG7), buildings and transport (SDG 11), waste management (SDG12), and biodiversity (SDGs 14 and 15).  Significant emphasis was also placed on situating the NDCs as entry points to reduce inequalities (SDG10) and advance gender equality (SDG5), in line with national needs and priorities and within the context of their cooperation frameworks.

ILO estimates indicate that 3.8 billion people globally lack access to any form of social protection, while closing this gap would require an additional US$1.4 trillion in public financing. At the same time, the global jobs gap—people willing to work but unable to find employment—is projected to reach 400–408 million by 2026. Against this backdrop, the programme aims to strengthen support by United Nations Country Teams to safeguard lives and livelihoods in the face of the long‑term socio‑economic impacts of crises. The programme is aligned with the commitments of the Second World Social Summit for Social Development, contained in resolution 80/5, which reaffirm the imperative of full and productive employment, decent work for all, and universal, inclusive and sustainable social protection systems.
Lessons learned and planned change

The lesson for the programme was the need for stronger integration between employment and social protection policies, robust and sustainable financing frameworks to underpin scale‑up efforts, and enhanced multilateral cooperation between the United Nations and international financial institutions. In applying the lesson, the programme will promote a more coordinated United Nations approach to social protection and employment, support countries in developing integrated policy frameworks and strategies, and assist in identifying innovative financing options. Through strengthened policy coherence, financing, and programming support, the programme will enable increased investment in social protection and livelihoods and accelerate progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals.

text: XIV.	United Nations Youth Office

children.text: A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The United Nations has long recognized that the imagination, ideals and energy of young people are vital for the continuing development of the societies in which they live. In 1965, in its resolution 2037 (XX), the General Assembly acknowledged the Declaration on the Promotion among Youth of the Ideals of Peace, Mutual Respect and Understanding between Peoples. In 1995, the Assembly adopted the World Programme of Action for Youth to the Year 2000 and Beyond in its resolution 50/81, which provided a policy framework and practical guidelines to improve the situation of young people. In 2007, the Assembly adopted the Supplement to the World Programme of Action for Youth to the Year 2000 and Beyond in its resolution 62/126, which provided further guidance on promoting the participation of young people in social and economic development. Since 2015, the Security Council, in its resolutions 2250 (2015), 2419 (2018) and 2535 (2020), has called upon all relevant actors to increase the inclusive representation of young people in the prevention and resolution of conflict, including when negotiating and implementing peace agreements.

In 2013, the Secretary-General appointed the first Envoy on Youth. In 2018, to strengthen the coordination and accountability of the United Nations system with regard to its work on young people, the Secretary-General launched the United Nations Youth Strategy. The General Assembly, in its resolution 76/306, decided to establish the United Nations Youth Office as a dedicated office for youth affairs in the Secretariat, integrating the Office of the Secretary-General’s Envoy on Youth. On 27 October 2023, the Secretary-General appointed the first-ever Assistant Secretary-General for Youth Affairs to lead the Office, representing the youngest serving Assistant Secretary-General in the history of the Organization. The mandate derives from the priorities established in relevant resolutions and decisions of the Assembly and the Security Council, including Assembly resolutions 50/81, 62/126, 76/306, 77/336 and 78/179 and Council resolutions 2250 (2015), 2419 (2018), 2535 (2020) and 2807 (2025)  .
Programme of work
Objective

The objective, to which the Office contributes, is to ensure the meaningful engagement and leadership of young people in the work of the United Nations and accelerated action at the global, regional and country levels to empower young people, promote their rights and address their needs.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the Office will:

(a)	Lead engagement and advocacy for the advancement of youth issues across the United Nations in the areas of peace and security, sustainable development and human rights, through engagement with Member State representatives, principals of United Nations organs and senior management of United Nations entities, and in close consultation with young people;

(b)	Promote meaningful, inclusive and effective engagement of young people and of youth-led and youth-focused organizations in the work of the United Nations, in close collaboration with United Nations system entities;

(c)	Encourage greater United Nations system-wide collaboration, coordination and accountability on the advancement of youth issues, including United Nations support to Member States, as appropriate and upon request, in promoting the effective and meaningful engagement, participation and empowerment of young people;
(d)	Engage with youth-focused envoys, representatives and offices of regional organizations on advancing youth issues;

(e)	Propose innovative approaches to advance multi-stakeholder initiatives on the engagement and empowerment of young people, for the consideration of Member States, including on quality and inclusive education, decent jobs, skills development, digital transformation and youth-led innovation and solutions;

(f)	Promote and facilitate intergenerational and intercultural dialogue, collaboration and solidarity by creating opportunities for young people to not only share and collaborate among one another, but also engage with Member States, the private sector, academia and the United Nations, including through intergovernmental policy forums;

(g)	Support efforts to enhance youth representation at the United Nations, including through increasing and improving the conditions of internships and employment opportunities for young people, especially for those from developing countries and with due regard to gender balance;

(h)	Support efforts towards the mobilization of financial and technical support and investment to promote and upscale quality and inclusive education and training, skills development, capacity-building and bridging the digital divide, in tandem with job creation, for young people and creating an enabling environment for harnessing their talents and abilities to contribute to their societies;

(i)	Conduct outreach to young people and to youth-led and youth-focused organizations, through innovative means, including the use of social media, narrative storytelling and audiovisual content, with an emphasis on the creation of multilingual assets and templates, where possible, for global dissemination through United Nations country teams and United Nations information centres.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:
(a) 	Meaningful youth engagement being systematically integrated into governance structures, policymaking and decision-making processes at the intergovernmental, regional and national, levels;
(b)	Strengthened coherence, accountability and collaboration on youth issues across the United Nations system;

(c)	Enhanced mechanisms and increased investments being made available to support socioeconomic opportunities for young people, across social, economic and environmental priorities at the global, regional and national levels.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a)	Member States continue to support the advancement of the situation of young people, including in the implementation of relevant international frameworks and agreements;
(b)	Sustained recognition by the global community of the important role that young people play in the promotion of peace and security, sustainable development and human rights;
(c)	There is adequate allocation of resources for action on young people and meaningful youth engagement across the United Nations system and national, regional and global institutions.

With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, the Office will collaborate with regional and national youth authorities, envoys and regional organizations. It will also prioritize the forging of new relationships and the strengthening of existing collaboration with relevant youth organizations, civil society organizations, academia and the private sector.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Office will continue to coordinate more than 60 United Nations entities and all United Nations country teams for improved collaboration, coherence and accountability in youth work across the United Nations system under the United Nations Youth Strategy (Youth2030). The Office will provide secretariat support to the strategy’s High-level Steering Committee and the joint working group responsible for advancing coherent action by the United Nations system on youth-related matters.  It will also continue to work with the Department of Management Strategy, Policy and Compliance, the Department of Operational Support and other members of the United Nations Youth Strategy to improve internships and employment opportunities across the United Nations system and beyond, with a focus on advancing socioeconomic opportunities for young people. It will collaborate with the Department of Global Communications to elevate the Organization’s work with and for youth and advocate for their rights, participation and protection. It will continue to exercise its system-wide lead in Youth2030 to advance the Youth, Peace and Security agenda across the United Nations, in line with Security Council resolution 2807 (2025) and the UN Youth Office Strategic Plan 2025–2028. Building on its engagement in the inter-agency joint secretariat on the Youth, Peace and Security agenda, alongside UNFPA and DPPA/PBSO, and through systematic global-level engagement—with intentional linkages to regional and national processes—the Office will advocate for and support the translation of the Youth, Peace and Security commitments into practice, including through structured engagement with Member States, parliamentarians, and regional organizations. It will also contribute regularly to the work of various inter-agency working groups and partner with relevant United Nations entities, as mandated, on meaningful youth participation in major intergovernmental meetings and across the UN system, to accelerate innovative governance models and advocate for global action on youth inclusion and youth leadership. As part of the efforts to strengthen support for young people, the Office will continue to collaborate with OHCHR, including on advancing mental health as a human right.

The Office integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate, by ensuring the meaningful participation of girls and young women in United Nations processes and intergovernmental decision-making, facilitating intergenerational discussions on women’s leadership, promoting the integration of a gender perspective into youth inclusion and youth-led action and by promoting discussions on sexual and reproductive health and rights as an integral part of the youth agenda.

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy and guided by the Office’s research findings and recommendations on young people with disabilities, the Office will advocate for meaningful participation of young persons with disabilities in the work of the United Nations and beyond. In consultation with young people with disabilities and their networks and organizations, the Office will mainstream disability inclusion into all aspects of its work, with the aim of ensuring accessibility to opportunities, information and events, to the greatest extent possible.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 initiative

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects efforts of the Office to implement all mandates in a more efficient and effective manner and contains no substantive adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative.

The Office will be guided by any future decisions taken in the context of the UN80 Initiative, in accordance with the applicable rules and procedures, including decisions, resolutions and established practice of the competent intergovernmental organs.
Evaluation activities
A thematic evaluation on youth engagement, to be conducted by the Office of Internal Oversight Services (OIOS), is planned for 2027.
Programme performance in 2025
Progress in advancing youth priorities and meaningful youth engagement

In 2025, the UN Youth Office, through its flagship initiative, the UN Youth Compass — notably the global #YouthLead Festival and decentralized Dialogues — significantly expanded the scale and reach of youth engagement in global processes. The initiative engaged over 75,000 young people from 182 countries, enabling them to contribute to forward-looking policy discussions and elevating youth priorities across key global platforms. These contributions supported the integration of youth priorities into United Nations processes, including the launch of Youth2030 Phase 2 (2025–2030), which introduced strengthened accountability for meaningful youth engagement, with 67 per cent of performance areas rated “green” across UN Country Teams. They also informed the advancement of global principles for meaningful, inclusive and safe youth engagement under the Pact for the Future. Through these efforts, more structured and accountable approaches to youth engagement were strengthened, enabling young people to contribute to shaping global policy and sustainable development.

text: XV.	Office of Data Protection and Privacy

children.text: A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The Office of Data Protection and Privacy was established pursuant to General Assembly resolution 78/252 as an independent office responsible for assisting the Secretariat in ensuring respect for data protection and privacy in the use and processing of personal data by Secretariat entities, consistent with United Nations mandates. The right to privacy in contemporary international law is enshrined in multiple international frameworks, including article 12 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and article 17 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. The Assembly has continued to consider this issue actively, including through its resolution 77/211 and preceding resolutions, by which it reaffirmed the right to privacy in the digital age, and its resolution 78/265, in which it advocated for the safeguard of privacy and the protection of personal data as part of promoting safe, secure and trustworthy artificial intelligence systems. .

In furtherance of relevant resolutions and decisions of the General Assembly, the Secretary-General promulgated a bulletin by which he established a data protection and privacy policy for the Secretariat (ST/SGB/2024/3). The Office contributes to the effective implementation of data protection and privacy standards, in line with that policy, and to fostering a culture of data protection and privacy awareness across the Secretariat.
Programme of work
Objective

The objective, to which the Office contributes, is to ensure that, when personal data are processed by United Nations Secretariat entities, such processing is consistent with United Nations mandates and in a manner that respects the rights of individuals and groups.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the Office will:

(a) 	 Provide independent and impartial advice and support to the Secretary-General and United Nations Secretariat entities on the measures to be taken to ensure compliance with the data protection and privacy rules, regulations, processes and policies of the Secretariat;

(b)	Provide assistance to entities, for example, to fulfil requests made by individuals about their personal data to ensure implementation and compliance with relevant data protection and privacy rules, regulations, processes and policies in relation to personal data that are shared across entities, including through Secretariat-wide enterprise systems, or that otherwise relate to several entities;
(c)	Establish and maintain a reporting mechanism for receiving and disseminating requests made by individuals about their personal data;
(d)	Monitor and report to the Secretary-General on compliance with data protection and privacy rules, regulations, processes and policies of the Secretariat;
(e)	Foster a culture of data protection and privacy awareness across the Organization.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:
(a)	A workplace culture that recognizes the importance of data protection and privacy across the Secretariat;
(b)	Effective prevention, identification and mitigation of data protection and privacy risks across the Organization;
(c)	Increased transparency and accountability in the Organization’s data protection and privacy practices.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following assumptions:
(a)	United Nations Secretariat entities adopt data protection and privacy standards, in line with the data protection and privacy policy;
(b)	United Nations Secretariat entities utilize the standardized tools and frameworks provided by the Office to manage operational risk.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Office will participate in inter-agency networks, as appropriate, including with data protection and privacy officers of United Nations agencies, funds and programmes, to share best practices and advance common practices for data protection and privacy system-wide.

The Office integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results. For example, during the Organization-wide implementation of data protection and privacy requirements, the Office will ensure that the Organization’s personal data processing activities do not reinforce or exacerbate gender inequalities, or expose women, girls, or any other group at heightened risk of gender-based discrimination to harm.

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the Office will ensure that it takes into account the needs of persons with disabilities, both in the accessibility of its services and in its support for the implementation of the data protection and privacy requirements within the Organization. The Office will integrate disability inclusion considerations into the Organization-wide implementation of data protection and privacy requirements to ensure that the Organization’s personal data processing activities do not reinforce or exacerbate disability-related inequalities or expose persons with disabilities to harm. The Office will also work to ensure that any relevant content, including information conveyed online such as through privacy notices and forms, contains accessibility features that benefit persons with disabilities.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 initiative

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects efforts of the Office to implement all mandates in a more efficient and effective manner and contains no substantive adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative.

The Office will be guided by any future decisions taken in the context of the UN80 Initiative, in accordance with the applicable rules and procedures, including decisions, resolutions and established practice of the competent intergovernmental organs.
Evaluation activities

An evaluation to systematically and objectively assess the relevance, efficiency and effectiveness of the Office’s activities, with a view to informing programme performance and refining future targets, to be conducted by the Office, is planned for 2027.
Programme performance in 2025
Increased operational readiness in data protection and privacy management

Effective and coherent data protection and privacy management is essential to ensuring that personal data are handled responsibly across the Organization. In 2025, the Office facilitated a high-level review of the Organization’s data protection and privacy capabilities, which provided the necessary insights to refine priorities, identify areas requiring targeted support, and clarify key roles and reponsibilities across all levels. The high-level review of the Organization's data protection capabilities resulted in heightened awareness across Secretariat entities regarding the critical need for robust privacy frameworks and provided the necessary benchmarks to establish a meaningful, long-term strategy.

children.text: Result 3: Enhanced organizational resilience and data protection and privacy-by-design maturity in the age of artificial intelligence – Proposed programme plan for 2027

Effective data protection and privacy risk management is a core component of the Organization's data protection and privacy programme. The Office supports entities in the conduct of data impact assessments (DIA) to identify and mitigate risks, ensuring that these assessments are embedded in the design phase of personal data processing activities in line with the Data Protection and Privacy by Design (PbyD) principle. With the Organization’s growing reliance on technologies, including the expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) projects – including under the UN80 digital workstreams – there is a heightened need to integrate this risk management process systematically and early across relevant workstreams.
Lessons learned and planned change

The lesson for the Office was that manual, entity-level support on privacy is not scalable for the rapid, decentralized deployment of AI technologies across the Secretariat. In applying the lesson, the Office will pivot to a systemic oversight model. This involves embedding PbyD as a core operating principle for the Organization and deploying a standardized DIA toolkit to ensure high-velocity, low-friction accountability at the engineering stage. This transition will strengthen compliance, improve the systematic and timely identification of data protection and privacy risks, and reinforce centralized oversight for more effective mitigation.
