text: XVI.	Office for Digital and Emerging Technologies

children.text: A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

In an age of increasing digital interdependence, the General Assembly has long recognized that effective cooperation on technology issues is an indispensable component of addressing the new challenges and opportunities posed by an increasingly digitalized world, inter alia, in resolutions 56/183, 70/1, 70/125, 75/1, 78/132 and 78/160, including as a key driver for the implementation of the 2030 Agenda. The position of Envoy of the Secretary-General on Technology was established in 2021 to advise the senior leadership of the United Nations on key trends in technology, so as to guide the strategic approach taken by the Organization on such issues, to serve as an advocate and focal point for digital cooperation so that Member States, the technology industry, civil society and other stakeholders would have a first port of call for the broader United Nations system, and to facilitate multi-stakeholder policy dialogue on emerging technologies (see A/74/821). The establishment of the Office of the Envoy of the Secretary-General on Technology was noted by the Assembly in its resolution 75/316.

Through the adoption of the Global Digital Compact (resolution 79/1, annex I), the General Assembly requested the Secretary-General, following consultations with Member States, to submit a proposal to the Assembly for the establishment of an office, building on and incorporating the existing activities and resources of the existing Office of the Envoy of the Secretary-General on Technology, to facilitate system-wide coordination, working closely with existing mechanisms. In its resolution 79/258 A, the Assembly approved the establishment of the Office for Digital and Emerging Technologies and its operational functions. Through its resolution 80/173, the General Assembly reaffirmed the Office’s role to facilitate United Nations system-wide coordination on digital cooperation, working closely with existing mechanisms, and to support the follow-up to and implementation of the Global Digital Compact.
Programme of work
Objective
The objective, to which the Office contributes, is to ensure that cooperation on technology governance is advanced for a better future.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the Office will:
(a)	Advise the senior leadership of the United Nations on key trends in technology, so as to guide the strategic approach taken by the Organization on such issues;
(b)	Serve as an advocate and focal point for digital cooperation, through engagement with Member States, the technology industry, civil society and other stakeholders;
(c)	Facilitate multi-stakeholder policy dialogue on digital and emerging technology issues;
(d)	Strengthen system-wide coordination within and across the United Nations system on digital and emerging technology issues;
(e)	Support the follow-up and implementation of the Global Digital Compact.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:
(a)	More inclusive and effective cooperation at all levels on digital and emerging technology issues;
(b)	Strengthened coherence within and across the United Nations system on digital and emerging technology issues;
(c)	Enhanced implementation of the Global Digital Compact.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following assumptions:
(a)	Member States continue to engage in constructive dialogue and cooperation on digital and emerging technology issues at the global and regional levels;
(b)	Adequate extrabudgetary resources are available to ensure meaningful engagement across the United Nations system, and with national, regional and global institutions and organizations.

With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, the Office will collaborate with global and regional organizations, such as the World Bank, the African Union, the European Union and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. The Office will also prioritize the forging of new relationships and the strengthening of existing ones with relevant civil society organizations, academia and the private sector.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Office will strengthen system-wide coordination within and across the United Nations system on digital and emerging technology issues, promoting collective synergies and messaging on such issues, and reducing duplication for a more effective use of resources across the United Nations system. Such activities include serving as the coordinating entity for the Panel Secretariat supporting the United Nations Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence; coordinating, as required, a joint secretariat supporting the United Nations Global Dialogue on Artificial Governance, separate from that supporting the Panel; serving as Co-Chair of the Working Group on Digital Technologies with the International Telecommunication Union; strengthening coordination within and between the processes for the implementation of the Global Digital Compact and the outcomes of the 20-year review of the World Summit on the Information Society, as well as other United Nations processes, such as the multi-stakeholder forum on science, technology and innovation for the Sustainable Development Goals, and coordination with the Technology Bank for the Least Developed Countries; and partnering with and connecting other United Nations system and non-United Nations entities through joint programming towards the Office’s objective. The Office will also advance engagement with the regional economic commissions, the Development Coordination Office and the resident coordinator system to provide guidance on best practices regarding digital transformation for use by Member States, and for connecting to regional, national and local networks in support of implementation of the Global Digital Compact.

The Office integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate, including by advocating for the meaningful participation of girls and young women in relevant United Nations processes, and by incorporating a gender perspective on digital and emerging technology issues in multi-stakeholder policy dialogues facilitated by the Office.

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the Office will advocate for the meaningful participation of persons with disabilities in relevant United Nations processes and incorporate the perspectives of persons with disabilities on digital and emerging technology issues in multi-stakeholder policy dialogues facilitated by the Office. The Office will aim to ensure accessibility for persons with disabilities to information produced and events organized by the Office, to the greatest extent possible.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects efforts of the Office to implement all mandates in a more efficient and effective manner and contains no substantive adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative.

The Office will be guided by any future decisions taken in the context of the UN80 Initiative, in accordance with the applicable rules and procedures, including decisions, resolutions and established practice of the competent intergovernmental organs.
Evaluation activities
The following evaluation completed in 2025 has guided the proposed programme plan for 2027:
(a) Self-evaluation of ODET’s capacity to support resident coordinators for an improved localised implementation of the Global Digital Compact.

In response to the results of the evaluation referenced above, the Office will continue providing guidance to resident coordinators to support the localized follow-up and implementation of the Global Digital Compact. In addition, the Office will seek to facilitate a workshop at the annual resident coordinators retreat.
A self-evaluation of the Office regarding its role in facilitating United Nations system-wide coordination on digital cooperation and digital and emerging technology issues is planned for 2027.
Programme performance in 2025
Progress on the Global Digital Compact becomes visible to all stakeholders

The commitments in the Global Digital Compact require significant collective action to achieve its ambitious goals. In 2025, the Office launched the UN Digital Cooperation Portal, which significantly enhanced the opportunities for all stakeholders to map digital initiatives, connect to global partners, and track progress on key priorities.

In line with ODET’s operational function to strengthen system-wide coordination, the portal brings together more than fifteen UN system entities and numerous stakeholders to present their progress across the five Global Digital Compact objectives. Besides showcasing UN system contributions, the portal has become a helpful tracker for external Compact implementation, making use of publicly available resources to show a global summary of initiatives by objective. The portal also offers an innovative suite of resources, compiled under an “AI Toolbox”. To increase alignment with the Global Digital Compact, the platform enables users to demonstrate how their initiatives integrate its objectives and to build a coherent narrative around it.

Through the adoption of the Global Digital Compact (resolution 79/1, annex I) in September 2024, the General Assembly committed to establishing a multidisciplinary Independent International Scientific Panel on AI and initiating a Global Dialogue on AI Governance within the United Nations. Through its resolution 79/325 in August 2025 on the terms of reference and modalities for the establishment and functioning of this Panel and Dialogue, the Assembly established these mechanisms within the United Nations and requested the Secretary-General to facilitate appropriate Secretariat support for each, within existing mandates. In September 2025, the Office supported the high-level multi-stakeholder informal meeting to launch the Dialogue in the margins of high-level week. The Office also coordinated across the UN system and administered the implementation of the Secretary-General’s criteria-based open call to recommend a list of 40 members for the Panel for appointment by the General Assembly, alongside measures to safeguard the Panel’s scientific independence including administering the mandated conflict of interest disclosure procedure. In February 2026, the General Assembly appointed the members of the Panel for a term of three years. The Office was also assigned the role of coordinating entity for the Panel Secretariat supporting the Panel, in line with Assembly resolution 79/325.
Lessons learned and planned change

The lesson for the Office was that effective Secretariat support to global, multi-stakeholder mechanisms on artificial intelligence requires clear administrative and operational frameworks, early coordination, and sustained system-wide engagement to ensure timely and high-quality delivery in conformity with mandates. In applying the lesson, the Office will continue to serve as the coordinating entity of the Panel Secretariat, and coordinate the separate Dialogue joint secretariat as required, by leveraging United Nations system-wide capacities, and providing and coordinating operational and other support for each mechanism. The Office will ensure that Secretariat support for the Panel serves to safeguard the scientific independence of its work and reports, including through administering the ongoing conflict of interest disclosure process and other relevant measures. The Office will also continue to serve as an advocate and focal point for digital cooperation on artificial intelligence capacity-building, including by taking into consideration the contributions of the Panel and the Dialogue, supporting voluntary and transparent cooperation frameworks or initiatives, and advancing the development of international partnerships on artificial intelligence capacity-building in line with the Global Digital Compact.

text: XVII.	United Nations Alliance of Civilizations

children.text: A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027 and programme performance in 2025
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The United Nations Alliance of Civilizations was established in 2005, as an initiative of the Secretary-General, to explore the root causes of polarization within and between societies and to recommend a programme of action, including through the promotion of intercultural and interreligious dialogue to build bridges of understanding. The Alliance aims to foster understanding and cooperation across cultures and religions and to counter polarization and extremism.

The General Assembly, through its resolutions 64/14 and 69/312, expressed its support for the work of the Alliance and reiterated its valuable role in promoting greater understanding and respect among civilizations, cultures, religions and beliefs.

In its resolution 78/264, the General Assembly requested the Secretary-General to appoint a United Nations Special Envoy to combat Islamophobia. Subsequently, in its resolution 79/258 B, the Assembly approved the conversion of the post of High Representative for the United Nations Alliance of Civilizations (Under-Secretary-General), previously funded from extrabudgetary resources, to regular budget funding under the Alliance under section 1. The post serves a dual role as High Representative for the United Nations Alliance of Civilizations and the United Nations Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia.
Programme of work
Objective

The objective, to which the Alliance contributes, is to improve understanding and cooperation among nations and peoples across cultures and religions and to reduce polarization at the local and global levels.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the Alliance will:
(a)	Promote interreligious and intercultural dialogue, including dialogue among civilizations;

(b) 	Design and implement peace education initiatives aimed at equipping young people with the critical thinking skills and competencies needed to play an active and positive role in issues of peace and security and in preventing violent extremism and radicalization;

(c)		Provide a grant funding mechanism, capacity-building support and mentorship for young people, youth-led organisations and civil society organizations that implement projects related to intercultural and interfaith dialogue, particularly in areas affected by identity-based conflict, with a view to combating intolerance and stereotyping based on religion or belief;

(d)	Facilitate dialogues to build stronger partnerships and promote the voices of young people and of civil society at large, including faith actors and grass-roots organizations, thereby fostering mutual understanding and collaboration across divides;

(e)	Reinforce synergies with international organizations that work for the integration of migrant communities and promote the role of municipalities and cities in building inclusive and resilient societies;

(f)	Develop initiatives that serve to train young people in multimedia storytelling and video production and facilitate collaborative media projects that unite young creators from different cultural and religious backgrounds, with an emphasis on the creation of content that changes the narrative around migrants and promotes tolerance, respect, dialogue and cooperation;

(g)	Promote the role and contribution of women as peace mediators, including through the Women’s Alliance for Peace initiative and through intercultural and interreligious mediation training aimed at women leaders in conflict contexts;
(h)	Identify, showcase and promote the role of religious leaders and faith-based organizations engaged in interreligious mediation;
(i)	Develop, support and participate in global communication, advocacy and programming initiatives aimed at amplifying the message of inclusion and peace through sports;

(j)	Collaborate with arts institutions, cultural organizations and educational institutions to integrate arts into broader advocacy efforts aimed at promoting tolerance, respect, dialogue and cooperation;

(k)	Engage with United Nations entities for a comprehensive and coordinated approach to addressing and responding to Islamophobia, antisemitism and other forms of intolerance based on religion and belief;

(l)	Conduct briefings for Member States to highlight the linkages between religious intolerance and human rights, and to contribute to efforts towards the effective development of system-wide responses to all forms of religious intolerance;

(m)	Organize tailored institutional events focused on trends in Islamophobia to provide a platform for a multi-stakeholder approach, including Member States, relevant United Nations entities, media providers, civil society and faith actors, in combating Islamophobia;
(n)	Engage in dialogue on Islamophobia with State and non-State actors, in order to address the root causes and explore possible solutions and good practices to address Islamophobia;

(o) 	Engage with Member States and relevant stakeholders to assist, as appropriate, in the implementation of the recommendations contained in the United Nations Plan of Action to Safeguard Religious Sites, including carrying out the “#forSafeWorship” communication campaign; raising the awareness of the international community and the general public about the universality of religious sites; and issuing press statements in condemnation of attacks on worshippers, acts of violence, and attacks on and destruction of religious places, sites and shrines, which are in violation of international law, in both conflict and non-conflict situations;

(p)	Engage with relevant United Nations entities and agencies on the implementation of the recommendations contained in the United Nations action plan to enhance monitoring and response to antisemitism, including the convening of relevant stakeholders (Member States, regional and international organizations, and Jewish organizations and communities) to explore good practices to respond to antisemitism.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:
(a)	Enhanced social stability and an environment conducive to peace and mutual understanding;
(b)	Advancement of intercultural and interreligious dialogue, and a culture of peace and mutual respect;
(c)	Improved action by Member States and non-State actors in addressing the root causes of all forms of religious intolerance, xenophobia and discrimination based on religion, belief or ethnicity.
With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the following planning assumptions:
(a)	Governments have the political commitment and dedicate resources to accelerate action to prevent conflicts and address the root causes of all forms of religious intolerance;
(b)	Civil society, faith-based organizations, local communities, the private sector and media are committed to working together to advance intercultural and interreligious dialogue;
(c)	Personnel, at all levels, prioritize addressing all forms of religious intolerance within United Nations operations.

With regard to cooperation with other entities at the global, regional, national and local levels, the Alliance of Civilizations will continue to garner the support of Member States for the advancement of intercultural and interreligious dialogue, a culture of peace and mutual respect, and for the reinforcement of partnerships with regional and subregional actors for the practical implementation of its activities, including with the European Union, the League of Arab States, the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, the Organization of American States, the Council of Europe, the Black Sea Economic Cooperation Organization, the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe, the International Organization of Turkic Culture and the Union for the Mediterranean. In addition, the Alliance will continue to work closely with non-State actors, namely civil society, young people, local communities, faith actors, academic institutions, the media, research institutes and the private sector, to build capacity and raise awareness of the role of intercultural and interreligious dialogue in conflict prevention and addressing the root causes of all forms of religious intolerance, xenophobia and discrimination based on religion, belief or ethnicity.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Alliance will continue to co-chair the United Nations Inter-Agency Task Force on Religion and Sustainable Development and engage its multi-faith advisory council; act as Vice-Chair of the Working Group on Preventing and Countering Violent Extremism Conducive to Terrorism; and lead the establishment and the activities of a United Nations working group to monitor, evaluate and assess the impact of policies and measures to address antisemitism on a regular basis. In addition, the Alliance will continue to strengthen its cooperation with the Department of Global Communications, the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs, the International Organization for Migration, the United Nations Population Fund, the Office of Counter-Terrorism, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, the Office of the Special Adviser to the Secretary-General on the Prevention of Genocide, OHCHR, the United Nations Youth Office and the Special Rapporteur on freedom of religion or belief through information exchange, joint events and initiatives, for more effective advocacy and coordinated actions to ensure that the prevention agenda remains prominent on the international agenda and to address all forms of religious intolerance in a coherent manner within the United Nations system.

The Alliance integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate. In 2027, it will continue to support the Women’s Alliance for Peace and promote the inclusion of women peace mediators in conflict mediation and conflict resolution initiatives. It will also continue its advocacy to ensure that the voices of young women and men that support peace processes at the local level are more actively represented at global events organized by the Alliance and other relevant forums. Information on the beneficiaries of the Alliance’s programmes will continue to be systematically disaggregated by sex in order to present a gender-sensitive analysis of the impact of the Alliance’s programme.

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the Alliance will seek to systematically integrate accessibility and reasonable accommodation considerations into the planning and delivery of its conferences, meetings, and capacity-building activities. It is important to strengthen coordination across the United Nations system and deepen engagement with Member States and non-State actors to address antisemitism, including Holocaust denial and distortion. The Alliance has been supporting stakeholder engagement in the implementation of the United Nations Action Plan to Enhance Monitoring and Response to Antisemitism, which provides recommendations to strengthen monitoring, education, public advocacy and coordinated responses to antisemitism across the United Nations system. Through enhanced collaboration among United Nations entities, Member States, Jewish organizations, faith actors, civil society organizations, educators, youth networks and digital platforms, the Action Plan seeks to support safer and more inclusive societies, improve awareness and understanding of antisemitism and strengthen efforts to counter antisemitic hate speech, attacks on Jewish communities and online manifestations of antisemitism.

The lesson for the Alliance was that effective efforts to combat antisemitism require sustained engagement with both State and non-State actors, as well as coordinated approaches that address the root causes of religious intolerance and hate speech. In applying the lesson, the Alliance will continue to facilitate consultations, partnerships and joint initiatives aimed at promoting mutual respect, protecting vulnerable communities and strengthening social cohesion and inclusion.

text: XVIII.	United Nations Sustainable Development Group System-Wide Evaluation Office

children.text: A.	Proposed programme plan for 2027
Overall orientation
Mandates and background

The United Nations Sustainable Development Group System-wide Evaluation Office is responsible for the provision of independent evaluation evidence that can be used to strengthen learning, transparency and accountability, and to incentivize joint work. As a unique function within the United Nations development system, the work of the Office provides a whole-of-United Nations approach to assess the combined contributions to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. The Office conducts evaluations and syntheses to provide insights and learning focused on strategic priorities that cannot be adequately addressed through existing accountability mechanisms or evaluation functions.

In its resolution 70/1, the General Assembly called for transformative and collaborative action by the United Nations development system. To respond to that imperative, the Assembly, in its resolution 71/243 on the quadrennial comprehensive policy review of operational activities for development of the United Nations system, called for reform of the United Nations development system to support the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals. The Assembly also underscored “the importance of strengthening a high-quality, independent and impartial system-wide evaluation mechanism of operational activities for development that enhances coherence and interdependence in the overall evaluation architecture of the United Nations development system”.

In his report entitled “Repositioning the United Nations development system to deliver on the 2030 Agenda: our promise for dignity, prosperity and peace on a healthy planet” (A/72/684-E/2018/7), the Secretary-General set out his plan to make the United Nations development system more strategic, accountable, collaborative and responsive to national development needs and priorities, including through the establishment of an independent system-wide evaluation office.

The General Assembly, in its resolution 72/279, welcomed the strengthening of independent system-wide evaluation measures by the Secretary-General, including measures to improve capacities. Subsequently, in its resolution 76/4, the Assembly requested the Secretary-General to provide Member States with the information needed to fully support and facilitate the establishment and functioning of an independent and well-resourced evaluation office as a critical accountability tool. The Secretary-General has provided this information in his regular reports to the Assembly and the Economic and Social Council on the implementation of the quadrennial comprehensive policy review of operational activities for development of the United Nations system (A/73/63-E/2018/8, A/74/73-/E/2019/14, A/75/79-E/2020/55, A/76/75-E/2021/57, A/77/69-E/2022/47 and A/80/74-E/2025/53).

After a transition arrangement was put in place in 2019, the Secretary-General appointed the first Executive Director of the Office in 2023, reporting directly to the Secretary-General. The Economic and Social Council, in its resolution 2023/31, noted the establishment of the Office and looked forward to updates on its functioning and work.  The Office operates in accordance with the United Nations Sustainable Development Group (UNSDG) System-Wide Evaluation Policy which was adopted by the UNSDG in November 2024. The policy sets out its mandate in relation to United Nations oversight bodies and evaluation offices and confirms authorities and reporting lines.

The General Assembly, in its resolution 79/226 requested that the Executive Director of the Office, beginning in 2025, present an annual report to the Economic and Social Council at its operational activities for development segment. The first of these reports (E/2025/57) was presented in 2025.
Programme of work
Objective

The objective, to which this Office contributes, is to advance the collective contribution of the United Nations development system to accelerate the implementation of the 2030 Agenda and the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals.
Strategy and external factors for 2027
To contribute to the objective, the Office will:

(a)	Conduct relevant, timely, credible and high-quality system-wide evaluations of development system results and performance to complement the evaluation work of United Nations entities, focused on activities that cannot be adequately addressed through existing accountability mechanisms, taking into consideration a gender perspective, disability inclusion, non-discrimination, human rights and environmental dimensions, as appropriate;
(b) 	Manage the evaluation of pooled funds and joint initiatives (in which several United Nations entities are working towards a common objective);

(c)	Promote increased collaboration on joint and system-wide evaluation, including by mapping the availability of evaluation evidence to inform the development of the Global System-Wide Evaluation Plan;

(d)	Enhance collective knowledge-sharing and learning through the production of syntheses and summaries of evaluation evidence across the United Nations system, and support the use of system-wide evaluation evidence to inform programme planning and the achievement of results across the United Nations development system;

(e)	Lead the implementation of the system-wide evaluation policy, providing advice and guidance for the system-wide evaluation function at the country, regional and global levels, including on the design and operationalization of evaluation quality assurance systems to support credible Cooperation Framework evaluations;

(f)	Implement systems to ensure efficient and effective evaluation management and follow-up, including to support evaluation quality and adherence to United Nations Evaluation Group norms and standards;

(g) 	Contribute to the work of the United Nations Evaluation Group and other partners to support the development of common technical guidance and the strengthening of evaluation capacity, including in relation to the generation and use of evidence to inform national progress towards the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals, in line with the role of evaluation envisaged in the 2030 Agenda.
The above-mentioned work is expected to result in:

(a)	Increased learning and accountability of development activities at the national, regional and global levels, to contribute to consistent implementation of system-wide priorities, policies and approaches across United Nations sustainable development system entities;
(b)	Strengthened capacities and use of system-wide evaluation evidence to inform programme planning and the achievement of results across United Nations development system entities;
(c)  	Complementarity and subsidiarity of system-wide evaluation with the work of United Nations evaluation, oversight and accountability mechanisms.

With regard to the external factors, the overall plan for 2027 is based on the assumption that adequate voluntary contributions are available to complement regular budget resources to carry out the activities of the Office.

With regard to cooperation at the global, regional national and local levels, the Office will collaborate with other international evaluation entities. The Office will participate as a member of the United Nations Evaluation Group and cooperate with the United Nations System Staff College to contribute to the development of common technical guidance and to evaluation capacity strengthening.

With regard to inter-agency coordination and liaison, the Office will coordinate its work with the Office of Internal Oversight Services, the Joint Inspection Unit and the Board of Auditors; and collaborate with the evaluation offices of United Nations entities to enhance coherence and leverage their work to maximise existing capacities and minimise costs in the conduct of system-wide evaluation activities.

The Office integrates a gender perspective into its operational activities, deliverables and results, as appropriate, including implementing guidance on mainstreaming a gender perspective into activities.

In line with the United Nations Disability Inclusion Strategy, the Office will integrate disability inclusion across all stages of its evaluation activities, in accordance with guidance of the United Nations Evaluation Group.
Adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative

The proposed programme plan for 2027 reflects efforts of the Office to implement all mandates in a more efficient and effective manner and contains no substantive adjustments arising from the UN80 Initiative.

The Office will be guided by any future decisions taken in the context of the UN80 Initiative, in accordance with the applicable rules and procedures, including decisions, resolutions and established practice of the competent intergovernmental organs.
Programme performance in 2025
System-wide evaluation evidence informs UN80 Initiative decision-making

The shift towards a “new generation of United Nations country teams” was a key priority of the repositioning of the United Nations development system, as set out in General Assembly resolution 72/279. In 2025, the Office completed a system-wide evaluation of progress towards this priority (SWEO/2025/001). The system-wide evaluation identified critical factors that support or hinder progress, providing independent evidence relevant to Workstreams 2 and 3 of the UN80 Initiative and the key priorities set out in General Assembly resolution 79/226 on the quadrennial comprehensive policy review. Based on these findings, the evaluation made seven strategic recommendations to close the gap between strategic vision and operational reality, addressing implementation challenges and structural barriers across the UN development system. The UNSDG accepted all seven recommendations, with follow-up actions embedded within the relevant work-packages of the ongoing UN80 Initiative.

children.text: Result 2: Improved use of United Nations system evaluation evidence by Member States and intergovernmental bodies for decision-making
Proposed programme plan for 2027

Bridging the gap between the production of evaluation evidence by United Nations entities and its strategic use by intergovernmental bodies and United Nations leadership is important for accountability and learning. The Office has completed a pilot initiative on use of demand-driven tools and approaches, drawing on artificial intelligence, to simplify and accelerate the system-wide mapping and use of the large volume of evaluations produced annually across the United Nations development system.
Lessons learned and planned change

The lesson for the Office was that while there is an extensive body of United Nations evaluation evidence, it is fragmented and challenging for stakeholders to access and consider collectively, limiting its contribution to collective learning. In applying the lesson, the Office will strengthen the use of, and learning from, this body of evaluation evidence by preparing timely, accessible and user-friendly knowledge products and dissemination tools, including syntheses, summaries, and evidence maps. This aims to: (a) improve equitable access to United Nations evaluation evidence and learning at the country level; and (b) strengthen the link between operational activities and intergovernmental processes, contributing to a shared understanding of how the development system is delivering, what improvements are needed, and how collective action can be strengthened to accelerate progress towards the SDGs.

Reclassification of 1 post of Under-Secretary-General to Assistant Secretary-General

The proposed downward reclassification of the post of Under-Secretary-General to Assistant Secretary-General, effective 1 September 2027, takes into account operative paragraphs 15 and 16 of General Assembly resolution 80/242 and the Assembly’s request to maintain the momentum of the UN80 initiative and reduce or reclassify the overall number of senior level posts.
United Nations Sustainable Development Group System-wide Evaluation Office

Conversion of 5 posts, comprising 1 post of Executive Director (D-2), 2 posts of Evaluation Officer (P-4), 1 post of Associate Evaluation Officer (P-2) and 1 post of Programme Management Assistant (GS (OL))

The proposed conversion of five posts, previously funded from extrabudgetary resources to the regular budget, follows a review of the current funding arrangements, the anticipated decrease in extrabudgetary resources and the need to ensure a more transparent and sustainable funding arrangement to underpin two core design features of the Office: independence and transparency. The role played by the Executive Director and her Office incentivizes joint work and collective learning among United Nations development system entities. The Office conducts and advances system-wide evaluative evidence on the United Nations development system’s contribution to the implementation of the 2030 Agenda.

The incumbent would provide leadership and strategic guidance for the system-wide evaluation function. Functions would include developing, managing and administering the programme of work of the Office; implementing systems to support evaluation quality and utility; enhancing capacities and promoting collective knowledge-sharing and learning; and ensuring coordination with United Nations oversight bodies and other entities.

The incumbents would be responsible for managing and conducting evaluations and leading evaluation teams, including planning and design; collecting, analysing and interpreting data; drafting terms of reference, inception reports and evaluation reports; and quality assurance.

The incumbent would be responsible for providing high quality and timely support to the management and conduct of system-wide evaluations, including planning and design; collecting, researching, analysing and interpreting data; and drafting terms of reference and evaluation reports.

The incumbent would support the Office and be the focal point for the provision of administrative services necessary for the successful functioning of all required office systems, including the management of information, budget overview, funds commitments and organisation of evaluation missions and workshops.
